speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Secretary of State for Exernal Affairs, in connection with the prime ministers' conference in the city of London, whether the stand of the Canadian government now is that the situation in Rhodesia is a dangerous and difficult one, and that it should be dealt with by the prime ministers' conference rather than being submitted to the United Nations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Rhodesia at the prime ministers' conference began, as we all know, the day before yesterday. It is possible that the Prime Minister
September 8, 1966

will be making an intervention later today or tomorrow. speakername: Hon. Paul  Marlin@Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Apparently the minister has not been informed of what the Prime Minister said on arrival in the United Kingdom, as reported in the London Times of Tuesday, which says:
Refusing to commit either himself or his country-

subtopic: CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS-CANADIAN STAND ON RHODESIA
speechtext: Order, please. The right hon. gentleman knows that according to the rules he cannot quote directly from the report on which he wishes to base his question.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had to refer to what was reported in the London Times so I could bring it to the attention of the minister. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS-CANADIAN STAND ON RHODESIA
speechtext: At the opening of this conference the position of a good number of the countries in the Commonwealth was that it would be desirable if possible to try to bring about a solution of the Rhodesia problem within the Commonwealth. I believe this is something for which we all would aim. This does not, of course, preclude the possibility of examining a resort to procedures which might be available under the charter of the United Nations. I am not saying that resort will be made to such procedures, but in the discussion which is now underway there will undoubtedly be proposals calling for an examination of alternatives.

subtopic: CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS-CANADIAN STAND ON RHODESIA
speechtext:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS-CANADIAN STAND ON RHODESIA
speechtext: We all have our views as to what would be the wisest course, but I think instead of declaring these views while the conference is in progress it would be better to suspend judgment.

subtopic: CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS-CANADIAN STAND ON RHODESIA

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, September 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickersgill for the second reading of Bill No. C-231, to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
If the minister speaks now he will close the debate. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of
the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a comparatively limited number of observations on this important bill. It covers a subject that has been before parliament on a number of occasions and the subject of a series of royal commissions. The problems surrounding the bill's application have been fully discussed by members of all parties and in particular by members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. The detailed examination given by members indicates the attitude of the opposition about a problem of deep significance. It is one requiring the fullest consideration and discussion by the committee when it is set up.
The bill is of a complexity that makes necessary complete and thorough examination. In committee hearings I hope that counsel will be provided to ensure that representative groups will be assured that their evidence will receive fullest consideration and in the presentation of it they will have the benefit of counsel learned in this abstruse field of the public service.
In 1931, under the prime ministership of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, a commission was set up to inquire into transportation in Canada, particularly in relation to railways, shipping and communication facilities, having regard to
Transportation
present conditions and probable future development, and to report their conclusions and make such recommendations as they thought proper. The order in council gave an indication of the comprehensive nature of the transportation problem:
-the vital importance of transportation to the trade and commerce of Canada, the serious and continuing deficits of the C.N.R. system, and the diminished revenues of the C.P.R. system, conditions which have been brought about, in part, by duplication of tracks, facilities and services of every kind, and in part by competition by other modes of transportation, particularly motor vehicles operating on highways-
Reference to that order in council is indicative of the fact that the problem has changed little in 35 years. The Duff commission on September 13, 1932, recommended:
-affording early relief to the federal treasury by reducing the alarming and increasing deficits and the demands for further capital expenditure in connection with the C.N.R. system.
Through the years the problem has remained unsolved and indeed insoluble. In conclusion the 1932 report stated:
We feel compelled, as a matter of public duty, to strike a serious note of warning to the people of Canada. Unless this country is prepared to adopt the plan we have proposed, or some other equally effective measures, to secure the economical and efficient working of both railway systems and thereby not only reduce the burden on the federal treasury but improve the financial position of the privately owned railway, then the only courses left would be either to effect savings in national expenditure in other directions, or to add still further to the burdens under which the industries of the country are suffering by the imposition of yet further taxation-
I refer to this because there are those who would have us believe this problem has developed only recently. When we on this side were charged with the administration of affairs, we decided, as a matter of major importance, in order to bring about development on a fair and equal basis in all parts of Canada, there must be an examination in detail of the transportation problem. In particular, we decided, without other matters taking a secondary position, the discrimination in freight rates which has played havoc in western Canada and the maritimes should be studied in search of a fair and reasonable formula.
The order in council which set up that royal commission made it clear the removal of discrimination was of major importance. Time passed. The commission made its report. There have been some suggestions there was delay on the part of the government of

September 8, 1966
Transportation
that day. The first report of that commission was received in March and released on April 10 of 1961.
At that time the commission set forth the general principle that burdens which are the result of obligations imposed upon railroads by tradition, law and so on should be lifted. Its major recommendations were that there should be self-liquidation of subsidies starting at $97.3 million in 1961 and reducing gradually to $30 million in 1965 to meet the removal of distortions which have resulted from national obligations and so on, that unnecessary passenger services should be discontinued, and that branch lines which are unnecessary should be closed. A $13 million loan fund was recommended to be established to offset the cost of maintaining certain uneconomical branch lines during the 15 years of the transitional period. It also stated that the statutory rates on grain were considered to be too low and that in their place a subsidy of $23.3 million should be substituted.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
A second report was tabled on January 23, 1962. The recommendations included first, the removal of the $7 million bridge subsidy on rail shipments across northern Ontario, second, the withdrawal of federal subsidies on goods moved by rail within the maritime provinces and, third, the appointment of a national transportation advisory council to report to the Minister of Transport and be responsible for assessing the impact of decisions made by all regulatory transportation agencies. Finally, it was recommended that there be the creation of a transportation statistics committee and the inauguration of an industrial freight traffic survey.
We had the legislation ready. It took some months to get that legislation ready, and in the fall of 1962 the undertaking was given that early in 1963 we would proceed with the legislation. We were defeated in the house, went to the country and a new government came into office. There was no delay or failure to take action for which we can be criticized, because we had to wait for reports.
That being so-and I have simply outlined some of the general considerations-what are the matters in issue?
The first, as I see it, is that if the legislation in its present form is not amended there will be continuing discrimination against the maritime provinces, the western provinces especially and northern Ontario in part. The railways will be all-powerful. They will be

able to exact, almost without limitation, anything the traffic will bear. That is a serious matter.
After the war there were increases of 157 per cent in freight rates across the board excepting within the limitations of the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Crowsnest pass arrangements. The result was that the discrimination of 1945 which in western Canada, according to my recollection, had begun at 17 per cent was accelerated by across-the-board additions to freight rates, thereby penalizing even more the western provinces. This again was subject to the terms and limitations provided under the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
Unless this present legislation is changed by parliament we will have in Canada for all time to come the injustice and distortion that result from certain areas of Canada having to pay freight rates far greater than other areas which have access to water or other transportation. This legislation cannot be accepted in its present form because it will result in continued unequal development of Canada.
This cannot be brushed aside. We cannot as Canadians, wherever we live, accept the principle that some parts of Canada are a noman's land for future development because of the acceptance of discrimination perpetuated in legislation. That is the first serious objection and one upon which I hope representatives from all parts of Canada will give evidence before the committee. This serious short coming must be rectified.
On the question of rationalization, I am seriously concerned about the results that will follow in the setting up of a board in name only, without power. The first thing the government should do, and I hope the minister will announce this today, is to have the railway companies withdraw applications made to date for the closing down of some 8,000 miles of railway lines across this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I think it is fundamental-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the right hon. gentleman would permit me-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister would allow me to continue. I know what he said the other day and I am asking him when he speaks today-on this occasion he is going
September 8. 1966

to follow me, apparently; I have often felt that I could give him some good leadership if he would do that in many other things-to deal with this question. The minister is going to follow me and then he will be able to answer. I know the undertaking that he gave the other day, but I should like to see the railways show their bona fides now by having the minister announce that these applications are withdrawn, not in the future, not when the committee is set up or is giving consideration to the matter, but now, because there will be grave injustice perpetrated unless action along this line is taken. An announcement by the minister today will show that we are not to accept the nebulous promises of the future as to action on the part of the railways in this regard. It could be explained clearly, that in consequence of representations made during this debate there will be action now to remove the overhanging fear facing various areas affected by the applications.
The third important matter is that there must be a body to control unjustifiable increases in freight rates. Are we going to hand over to the tender mercies of Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway the right to say: This is what we are going to charge, we can get away with it because there is no right of appeal or no effective appeal? They can charge whatever the traffic will bear.
That is a proposition I cannot accept.
What would be the consequence of such a proposition in connection with the tremendous developments that have taken place in potash mining in Saskatchewan, although I am not arguing this case from the point of view of western Canada alone but of the nation as a whole? When I was a boy these areas were regarded as completely unfit for cultivation. They were salt areas, alkali flats and the like. I know that the Minister of Transport is fully aware of this because the same situation prevailed in his area in Manitoba. We did not know that we had not a gold mine but a golden mine underneath our province and spreading to a lesser degree into the adjoining provinces.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
There can be no competition to keep down the price of freight on potash within Canada if this legislation is passed. It might be argued that there could be competition from the trucking companies. Trucks cannot meet the problem of transporting hundreds of millions
Transportation
of tons of potash, and in saying that I deliberately understate the potential of potash. We must not allow the removal of national direction in connection with freight rates. Is the government going to give to the railway companies-I mentioned potash as an example-the complete privilege of exacting whatever they wish without any limitation by competition? To do so will provide a field day for those who operate railway companies. Surely we have not come to that position yet.
I believe that we have imposed on rail transportation too much legislation and too many rules. Some of those rules must be revised but that does not mean that we should give to those kindly, gentle and philanthropic boards of directors of the great railway companies the power to make-Canadians pay through the nose where there is no competition to keep freight rates down.
I emphasize the need of a complete review not in the interest of one part of Canada but in the interest of the whole country. There is no reason why we who live in western Canada and those who live in the maritime provinces should be placed in a secondary position because of freight rates which will impose upon these areas to a far greater extent than on any other parts of the nation.
In this connection I think the editorial which appeared in the Telegraph Journal on; August 31 is of importance. It was headed: "National Transport Policy: This Area Must Be Alert." That was the view expressed by various maritime members during the progress of this debate. The editorial went on to say:
A national transportation policy based solely on "compensatory" freight rates-(i.e. keeping only profitable lines operating) could do immense harm to the maritimes.
It then continued:
So far, Ottawa seems to be keeping this in mind. It will be up to the Atlantic provinces to be sure their interests are protected as parliament legislates in this crucial field.
The next point I wish to raise is that we must not place the trucking industry of Canada in an unfair competitive position with the railways. The trucking industry is an industry of great importance in this nation. This legislation will continue to subsidize the railways within the limited areas which are referred to in the statutes but there is nothing that will protect the trucking companies from unfair or unjust competition.
I will give an example that has been brought to my attention of a case which

September 8, 1966
Transportation
cannot be justified. The case to which I am referring indicates the kind of injustice that this industry can suffer under the present laws. I am prepared to give the name of the company but I think the house will agree that in fairness it should not be mentioned. I will show the minister the letter in question so that the company's name will be available to him. This is a cartage company licensed for highway hauling. The letter reads in part:
I could give you many, many instances of rate cutting and agreed charges which have forced independent truckers out of business since 1959, but I will give you one complete example which happened to us.
The author of the letter then goes on to point out that a certain shipper was receiving poor and indifferent service from the railway and this company agreed to haul the freight at the rate of 82 cents per hundredweight. Three months later, after the company had begun hauling the commodity, it was advised that the C.N.R. had lowered its rate to 68 cents per hundredweight. The company agreed to continue at this rate. Two months later the company was advised that the C.N.R. had cut the rate to 55 cents per hundredweight and again it agreed to this rate. Two months later it was advised by the shipper that an agreed charge had been made with the C.N.R. which meant a further reduction.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
That is not fair competition. We subsidize the Canadian National but the truckers, as I see it, have no protection whatever. They are subject to competition such as this that is neither economic, just nor equitable. There must be within this legislation protection against that type of unjust competition which destroys private enterprise. Are we going to give the railways an open season on the Canadian consumer?
These are some of the problems that face the committee and which will require the most careful consideration. We had hoped that the amendment which we endeavoured to move yesterday would have been accepted. However, Your Honour ruled it out of order. I am impelled to say, although possibly I ought not to, that the way in which Your Honour has discharged the responsibilities placed upon him has added a new stature to the position of Speaker of this House of Commons.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Perhaps I should bring to the attention of the right hon. gentleman the fact

that I cannot claim credit for ruling the amendment out of order yesterday.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not confine my remarks to that. I think it was a decision in keeping with the traditions of the house. We were trying to have a principle determined. The hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) showed clearly that our purpose was not to defeat the bill but to improve the ultimate law that will be passed. I shall refer later today to the functions of an opposition because last evening in a broadcast the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) gave his considered opinion that an opposition is apparently to be seen and not heard, that the only trouble with the opposition is that it is too strong. If only the government had 175 members they would be able to tell the opposition to take that course which my respect for parliamentary rules forbids me to mention. A parliamentarian with the grace and distinction of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) or one with the wide knowledge of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) would never have made such a statement, I am sure, because that kind of statement is not a tribute to the parliamentary system. I do not believe in that doctrine.
I have mentioned this statement so I must quote it now in order that no one will say I have misstated the purport of the views of the Minister of Finance, who apparently was speaking for the government. He said:
I don't think that the opposition has been helpful to the government in restraining these pressures. Their attitude in the House of Commons has always been to put pressure on the government to make decisions quickly, to disregard what may be proper cautions-
I am living right up to that principle. I am saying, do not rush in with this legislation in its present form. Then Mr. Gordon, who was interviewing the minister, said:
More than legitimate pressures?
The minister replied:
I think so. And this wouldn't matter so much in a house in which we had the dominant majority, but we have slightly fewer than half the members, and therefore what happens in parliament today and the attitude of the opposition is far more important than it has ever been. If we were sitting there with 175 members we could ignore the opposition and say-*
I know that neither of the two ministers sitting on the front bench, to whom I have referred, would ever advance such a proposition. Then he went on to say-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Even with 208 you could not do it.
September 8, 1966

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman is not approving the statement made by the minister. The Minister of Finance then said:
-well, you know, that's just what you expect.
That is what the Minister of Finance would say to the opposition if he had 175 members-now, you can go to the other place with my compliments. This is clearly not the attitude to be expected from a minister of the crown, although it is indicative of a state of mind to which allusion has been made by members of the opposition on a number of occasions. I will amplify that later.
I hope that the Minister of Transport will not adopt those words in reference to the suggestions I am making for the purpose of rendering this legislation effective in the national interest. In its present form it cannot contribute to the unity of this country. It will simply accelerate the distortions of geographical growth and development, and the absence of competition will bring about concentration of industrial development in the central provinces to an even greater extent than is the case today. I hope the Minister of Transport will not adopt the curious, archaic and dictatorial attitude of the Minister of Finance as indicated in these words:
If we were sitting there with 175 members we could ignore the opposition and say: Well, you know, that's just what you expect.
I hope that the suggestions I have made will bring together the views expressed by many hon. members and I hope the views expressed by hon. members from this side of the house will receive the serious consideration of the government. There must be fairness, and there will be no fairness if discrimination, even if it came into being through the oversight of the Board of Transport Commissioners, is not to be entirely removed, and if an open season is to be declared on the consumers of Canada.
Now, sir, there is one other matter and that is the question of research. We hear a great deal today about the brain drain from Canada to the United States, about the thousands who leave for better opportunities in that country. It is also true that a number of people from the United States come to Canada, particularly in connection with the petroleum industry. However, there is a drain from this nation. What takes a highly trained man with unusual talents and abilities to a country other than his own? Some say it is better pay or material considerations. This
Transportation
can be explained in a general way as greater opportunity.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
That is the challenge that faces our country. You cannot strengthen political and national unity by accelerating freight and transportation rates in a way to perpetuate inequity.
We in Canada have fallen behind in the field of efficient, high-speed ground transportation. I see the minister agrees with that generalization; he has indicated his agreement. There are three areas in this country where the need for a positive policy is vital. There are the maritimes, to which I referred on an earlier occasion, the west coast of Canada and, believe it or not, Canada's industrial heartland, that narrow band of economic activity extending from Quebec City to Windsor.
So far as the maritimes are concerned, I have suggested, and I am not going to repeat it, that the railway line today is an anachronism, that what is needed is a faster and more direct connection between the maritimes and the industrial heartland. The present line runs from Montreal through Richmond, Levis, Mont Joli down to Moncton and is 840 miles in length. I suggested that a direct route from Richmond, Quebec, through the top corner of Maine to Woodstock, New Brunswick, and from there utilizing the present main line into Saint John and down to Moncton, would cut one-third off the distance. I am not going to give further details because I dealt with this matter on an earlier occasion, but the press in the maritimes has stated that this is a suggestion that deserves attention.
The west coast presents a different type of problem. I think the house is aware of the bottleneck impeding the convenient and efficient flow of goods to the port facilities of British Columbia. The Rocky Mountains have their scenic beauty but they contribute little to the transportation of goods. The mountains seriously hamper economic expansion of the prairies.
Rail facilities between British Columbia and the rest of Canada are no further advanced than they were 50 years ago. Despite the growth of Canada economically and in population, and despite the many technological achievements on virtually all fronts, we still have two companies with but one single railway track each linking the economic wealth and facilities of British Columbia with other parts of Canada.

September 8, 1966
Transportation
I believe we will have to catch the vision of further development, that we will have to build another rail line adjacent to those that exist today or, even though the cost be high, elsewhere, so that there will be additional tracks to carry the increased traffic that is bound to follow. On some future occasion I am going to deal with this matter in detail, but at the moment I am just trying to picture the kind of Canada we may have not many years hence if we catch something of the opportunities that are ours.
The third area that merits searching examination is Canada's industrial centre. It is my opinion, though hon. members may disagree with it, that within the next ten years the area in Canada between Quebec City and Windsor will be a 50-mile wide megalopolis. There will be a tremendous concentration within that area which will embrace 65 per cent of the population of Canada and 84 per cent of its industrial activity.
The railways have fallen far behind. They have simply carried on from year to year making technological changes and improvements to rolling stock but failing to envisage the greatness of Canada's future and the need for action now. I believe we must provide, within the area between Quebec City and Windsor which I have mentioned, the best ground transportation facilities possible. To fail will mean that we cannot take full advantage of the economic potential available. If our ground transportation is expensive, inefficient and disorganized, it will be a burden rather than a blessing to this highly sensitive industrial complex.
What should we do in order to meet the greatness of the transportation challenge? They laughed at Macdonald when he pictured the opening up of the west. Those who opposed said it would mean railroads from wigwam to wigwam. There was a revised version, Mr. Speaker, in 1958. When we placed before the people of Canada the opening of northern Canada, making available to the provinces the exploitation of great resources via our roads to resources program, it was said to be a concept of roads from igloo to igloo.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is the duty of government to provide certain basic services to facilitate the successful operations of free enterprise. A special research division of the federal Department of Transport is something that I have advocated for some time and I should now like to see it developed. There should be a most

exhaustive research program into all forms of ground transportation. We have never done that in Canada except in a haphazard way by one corporation or another. The research should be carried out in co-operation with private industry, the provincial governments and universities. We have badly neglected research in the field of ground transportation. When this legislation has gone through committee, it would be a massive step forward if the minister would set up a research program to give consideration to new vistas of opportunity for all parts of Canada, giving young Canadians something of that pioneering spirit of our forebears when they first devised our transportation system.
In the national interest action along these lines must be taken. If it is not taken, this legislation, when it is finally completed, will be merely an evanescent thing, lacking the impetus and inspiration that come from adoption of new ways and new opportunities.

Well, I am a yes-man; everybody knows that. The next point made by the Leader of the Opposition is a crucial one, a very crucial one indeed. He said that if there was no amendment to this bill the
September 8, 1966



railways would be all-powerful in the setting of rates. This is the first time I have to take issue seriously with the Leader'of the Opposition, but I have to take very serious issue because nothing is clearer than that the railways do not have the power to set rates except below a maximum in every case where someone can show he is a captive shipper. Any person, such as the shippers of potash who obviously cannot ship by truck or by any other means, obviously is a captive shipper. Every captive shipper is protected under this bill by a maximum rate. The railways will have no freedom to set a rate above this maximum. They will have freedom to give a lower rate than the maximum. Indeed, most large captive shippers today, by having agreed charges with the railways, do have rates which in fact I believe are somewhat lower and in some cases quite substantially lower than the maximum rate.
I do expect that in the committee we will have very serious debate about the maximum rate formula. It is a very large question and perhaps is a little more important to the prairies than to other parts of Canada, but not much. It is very important to many shippers in northern Ontario and in northern Quebec. As I say, when we come to examine this thing carefully I think we will find that most of those shippers will have protected themselves already by agreed charges, because they are very big shippers who have a considerable bargaining power of their own.
The only area in which the railways will be free under this legislation to set their rates is where there is effective competition. In our opinion, and in the opinion of Mr. MacPherson and also in the opinion of the previous government as reflected in the legislation they were about to introduce, effective competition will itself provide protection because nobody is going to be such a fool as to pay a higher rate to the railways than he can get from trucks, ships or any other effective competitor. Surely that is just ordinary common sense.

Not being an expert on these matters I would not attempt to give an answer to that. I am sure, however, that the hon. gentleman will be able to obtain an answer from someone far more competent than I ever will be in this field when we get into the consideration of this matter by the committee. What I am seeking to do here is to allay fears based on what I believe to have been genuine misunderstandings about the bill. The fact is that there will be, after this bill is passed, three or four different kinds of freight rates. There will be rates which are protected by the maximum rate formula, because the shipper can make no bargain of his own with the railways and therefore has the protection of the law. There will be agreed charges which are not in any way changed from the law as it now stands. There will be statutory rates such as the Crowsnest pass rates, the maritime freight rates and certain others. There will be competitive rates which will be based on the railways' judgment in respect of how they can get the business.
There is one very important thing I should like to say about these competitive rates, and this also deals with another point made by the right hon. gentleman. I refer to the question of the competition with trucks. In this bill it is provided that the railways must not carry goods at unremunerative rates. In other words, they must charge what it costs the railway to carry the goods. This is put in precisely because we do recognize that the railways are large and powerful and that many of their competitors will not have the same economic bargaining power. Therefore

September 8, 1966
Transportation
they are not allowed to use loss leaders to put people out of business.
Under the present law a competitor has no effective appeal. In this bill a trucker, believing the railway is seeking to put him out of business by quoting unremunerative rates, may appeal to the commission and have the matter adjudicated. So there will be a protection which does not exist at the present time. I think this is very important, because it would be a very bad thing indeed to permit a railway or any other powerful body to crush competition by this kind of practice and then find themselves in a position to raise rates again. This is a valuable protection.
The railways do not have any similar protection against the truckers. At the present time we do not think that is necessary because I do not think there are any trucking firms in Canada large and powerful enough to put the railways out of business. If they started charging unremunerative rates for any length of time, I imagine the people who would be put out of business would be the truckers themselves. What we are endeavouring to do is to make the bargaining powers relatively even in this connection.
A question which does arise and seems to bother a good many people has to do with the suggestion by me, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and by others that this legislation will permit the railways to earn more money than they are earning at the present time. Everybody seems to assume that the only way they can do that is by raising rates. I do not have any doubt that they will raise some rates if they can raise their competitive rates and still obtain the business, and I do not see why they should not because everybody else is allowed to do it. I do not see why they should not be allowed to go out, compete for business, take the burden off the taxpayers and let the users pay so long as there is an alternative for the shipper. I do not think this will happen especially in western Canada; I do not think it will happen especially in central Canada. I think it will happen all over the country.
I think the main virtue of this legislation is that the railways will be able to make bargains right away instead of having to file tariffs, wait 30 days, and be shackled by many things which make it impossible for them to run their railways in a business-like way. I would guess that much of the additional revenue they will get may come from cutting rates, not from raising them at all but

cutting them enough to get some of the business back.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We all know that the share of the freight that is being carried by the railways today compared with what it was before 1950 is lower. It is in fact very much smaller. This measure will give the railways a chance to compete. I think all those in the house who believe that competition and what we usually call freedom of enterprise are a good thing for the progress of the country should welcome this legislation. We are doing our best to see that there is complete protection for those who are not protected by competition. Where there is a monopoly situation the bill gives protection. Where there is a competitive situation we think the competition should give the protection. That is the attitude adopted to all other kinds of businesses and it does not seem an unreasonable one to take with respect to freight rates.
With respect to branch line abandonment the right hon. gentleman made an appeal to me to do something that I cannot do. He made an appeal to me to say here and now that the railways would withdraw their applications for abandonment right away, today. I assured the hon. member for Qu'Appelle the other day that the presidents of the railways had authorized me to tell the house that they would withdraw all these applications on the day on which this bill was passed by parliament. I think that was a reasonable position for them to take, because if the bill did not pass they would be just prejudging their position under the present law. Surely in fairness to them, until they know what parliament is going to do they should not be expected to withdraw these applications. But I do intend, as I told hon. members, early next week, I hope, or at any rate by the middle of the week to be able to send to every member of parliament the map showing the branch lines on the prairies, in fact, the whole network of lines, that the government intends, if this legislation passes, to guarantee will continue in operation until January 1, 1975. This map will show the network on which no applications will be considered for abandonment once this law is passed.
I should like to have given this map to hon. members today but I think I explained at the beginning of the debate, and this still applies, that there are one or two details I have to iron out with the officials and my colleagues before it is in final form. But it will be, I

There will still have to be applications which will still have to be considered by the commission, and the protection of the law will still be there in respect of those lines.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle was very helpful and constructive in this matter, as he has been in general with respect to this legislation. While the hon. gentleman did not agree with all the details of the branch line proposal, he felt that in general it will result in a very marked improvement in this connection. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the fact that the committee and the government regard the threat of inflation as an important and urgent matter is evidence that Canada will not drift into a period of continually rising prices and costs. As Minister of Finance with a special responsibility for the economic position of this country I welcome the opportunity afforded by this debate to place the facts of the situation before hon. members of all parties and before the public.
I might add, Mr. Chairman, that it is a remarkable but perhaps not surprising coincidence that today President Johnson has announced new steps that the United States is taking to curb inflationary pressures, some of these, I might add, of a character that we took some six months ago. I believe this indicates that throughout North America and throughout the world this is a matter that does demand the attention of legislators.
Here in Canada we have had a long and strong economic expansion in the past five and a half years. It has carried us from a condition of serious and persistent unemployment to one of widespread prosperity and virtually full employment. There is still too much unemployment in certain areas and among those who are poorly educated and unskilled, but this arises from reasons other than a shortage of opportunities in Canada taken as a whole. The total expenditures of money by consumers, by business, by government and by those who want our exports are now more than adequate to support a healthy level of economic growth.
Our main economic problems are now twofold: First, the longer term problems of educating and adapting our growing labour force and improving our capital resources to meet the opportunities presented in our modern world and, second, the shorter term problem

of preventing excessive total expenditures and excessive increases in prices and in costs of production. It is this second range of current problems which concerns the committee today and about which I will speak.
Canada's general record in regard to prices and costs during the past 30 years has been good. Our war finance and wartime price and wage control were effective and reasonably fair. During the period of decontrol and readjustment to peacetime conditions we suffered some inflation, as everyone else did. Much of it was inevitable as we readjusted to price levels in the United States and elsewhere.
During the Korean war in 1950 and 1951 prices rose too rapidly in Canada as well as elsewhere. I think now that we all should have done more to check them. Since that time, from 1952 until about a year ago, our prices were reasonably steady, rising over the period by an average of 1.4 per cent per year in the case of consumer prices, which was less than that of almost all other countries although slightly more than the United States.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This period covered the boom of the midfifties, the period of relatively high unemployment of the late fifties and early sixties and most of the recent long period of expansion. Over this period average hourly earnings of Canadian workers increased by an average of about 4 per cent per year, as shown by our statistics, and average personal incomes per capita for all Canadians by 4 per cent.
By the middle of last year it was evident that costs and prices in the field of construction were rising too rapidly, and in the summer of 1965 the government began to cut back its own construction programs to counteract this and urged others to do the same. We have kept this policy of restraint since that time, though it has not achieved as much success as I would like to have seen.
Speaking generally, Canadians have been very impatient to get on with very many things both directly and through their governments and now we are paying the price of trying to do too much all at once.
During the past 12 months the increases in costs and prices have been spreading in Canada as elsewhere. The chief cause is the continued rapid growth of total expenditures and a very high level of demand, which make it possible for labour and business to demand more and get it. There are Canadians in
September 8, 1966

almost all walks of life who seem to have reached the conclusion that now is the time to get more while the getting is good. As a result we have had accelerating increases in prices and costs, accompanied by urgent and pressing demands by special groups for more income, using whatever means are open to them.
We have now reached a position that is unstable. The present trends just cannot continue for long into the future. We cannot all get what we want and do what we want, and if everyone tries there is going to be an excessive rise in prices and in costs because right now the country just could not, no matter how hard it tries, produce enough to meet all the demands. If this kind of boom goes on, many will suffer as a result of higher prices and from the inevitable upset that will follow. All Canadians will suffer if a continued boom should lead to a bust. We must moderate our pace so that we can continue to grow in a steady way, with a continually increasing standard of living and with the economic and social improvements that we can afford year by year. Such moderation does not require that we cease to make progress toward social justice nor that those who have lacked opportunities must be left without help.
I should like to make this point because sometimes I think it is misunderstood. We in this country are the most fortunate people in the world. We have the means to make progress but we have got to pace our progress so that we do not exceed our means.
Let us bear in mind some simple facts. We are now producing about all we can in Canada this year. We have excellent market opportunities at home and in other countries. We have again been lucky in getting huge grain crops at a time when grains are in great demand. Our labour force is growing at a rate of a bit over 3 per cent a year and is becoming better educated and trained. Our productivity-the volume of goods and services per worker that we can produce-is growing somewhere between 2 and 3 per cent a year over all. Canadians can expect an increasing standard of living, on the average, which increases at a rate that bears some relationship to their average increase in productivity, say about 3 per cent a year over a long period.
By international standards this is a reasonable rate of increase. There are many countries that envy us very greatly. Those are
Supply-Finance
countries where standards of living are not rising at all because population is rising even more rapidly than the means of production. In Canada this rate of increase in productivity involves the doubling of the standard of living of the average Canadian within a generation. We have no reason to be anything but thankful to live in a country such as Canada.
If, however, some succeed by the strength of their position in getting substantially more than this increase in real income from year to year, others must get less than this increase. This applies to the owners of companies that sell goods to earn profits as well as those who sell their labour to earn salaries and wages.
We must also recognize that the average Canadian, although he is a fortunate citizen of the world and can look forward to a steadily rising standard of living, cannot have the same standard of living as the average United States citizen-at least not for some years. We just do not produce as much-we have not the same productivity in our industry-and we are not as rich in capital and technical capacity.
Our prices and wages are the result of bargaining and of market forces and of the efforts of individuals, businesses and groups to better their position. Prices are not held under control by governments either federal or provincial, apart from minor exceptions such as public utilities which enjoy monopoly positions. There are laws to prevent businesses from combining to increase or maintain their prices and profits. Such laws do not apply to workers, however, who are not only permitted but encouraged to organize and bargain collectively. This is one of the cornerstones of modern industrial democracy. On the whole this system has worked and has enabled great progress to be made in improving the incomes and status of workers. Parliament is engaged this session in setting up a framework for the extension to its own civil servants of this power to organize and bargain collectively, so it is clear we think well of it in principle.
Our experience this year, however, shows that these processes, whether they are the processes of making profits or the processes of bargaining for wages or salaries, by which Canadians increase their incomes have dangers as well as virtues. They can bring about excessive demands and excessive increases. They can promote inflation at the high levels of employment and low levels of unemployment which we have now achieved. It is clear

September 8, 1986
Supply-Finance
that if we are to succeed in maintaining high employment with price stability we must improve the working of our economy. We do not want to be forced to aim at a lower level of employment in order to avoid inflation. To me, this is the kind of cure for inflation that could be almost as bad as the disease and is to be avoided if at all possible. But to maintain high levels of employment without inflation is not a task for the government alone. It is only possible if business and workers will accept it as a serious objective and help to make it possible.
I think we would all agree that we should not let our economy persist in this rising and excessive rate of increase in prices and costs, including wages. But it is easier to reach that judgment than to implement it. What practical means can we use to check this rise and to get back on to a stable path of economic growth?
First we recognize that most of us do not want, and in any event we cannot impose, federal government control over prices and wages generally. This is only within parliament's powers during a national emergency such as war. In practice, price and wage controls would be unworkable in a diverse economy such as ours which is so actively engaged in foreign trade and based essentially on a free market system for business and collective bargaining for labour. I say this as one of those actively involved in the successful wartime price and wage controls. Moreover, we as politicians really do not want the responsibility for deciding on everyone's prices and wages. We would be in endless trouble. Our recent experience in trying to deal with railway wages is evidence enough on that point.
Second, we must consider the possibilities of an "incomes policy" such as some overseas countries have had, or "guideposts" for wage and price increases such as the United States has had. An incomes policy implies not a government control but the expression of government views to focus public opinion on changes in particular prices and particular wage disputes. It involves persuasion and if necessary criticism, with voluntary and systematic adherence to certain policies and standards. It would require, in Canada, cooperation between federal and provincial authorities and a willingness in the business world, as well as in unions and the ranks of labour, to follow voluntarily a central lead that enjoys a wide consensus of agreement and respect. While all these conditions do not now

prevail, I hope that in time we can meet these requirements, achieve this consensus and develop this kind of voluntary policy. But we cannot get an incomes policy now by merely voting for it here or advocating it. We have to work it out not only here in parliament, where we must develop attitudes and laws that will earn respect, but in the labour movement and the business world where private interests and processes of bargaining must be reconciled with a regard for the public interest.
As the house is aware, the government asked the Economic Council, which is representative of all the principal economic groups, to study the interrelationship between prices, costs, productivity and incomes, and to review policies and experiences of other countries in the world. I have just heard from the Economic Council that this report is expected late next month.When it is received the government plans to refer it to a parliamentary committee along with other matters to be raised in accordance with the notice on the order paper today. I should add that it has taken the Economic Council quite some time to study and discuss this problem, which is perhaps the best evidence of its inherent complexity and the need for reaching a consensus before we can proceed.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
As for guideposts, certain elementary considerations are self-evident. To achieve full stability of our consumer price level would require that our average increases in incomes per capita in Canada would have to be limited to about our over-all increase in productivity. To maintain the degree of price stability we have experienced on the average over the past ten years, it is evident from our productivity performance that we could not have increases in average incomes of more than four or five per cent a year. These facts of economic life, and they are facts, are some guide in themselves. Yet the typical increases taking place in money incomes in recent months have been in excess of this. Many current demands are much more. Many employers will have to grant large increases in the next few months simply to keep their men. We shall have to do so in certain categories of the public service. But somehow we must get back as soon as we can to more reasonable increases-average figures that do not exceed what I have mentioned. Some can, of course, be larger, as long as the average remains within reason.
September 8, 1968

What is needed, I feel, is a widespread understanding of the situation by the public, by business and by individual workers. Management, on its part, must make a special endeavour to keep prices down in order to dampen down and help bring to an end this spiral of price and wage increases. It would be helpful if some industries were to give the public the advantage of increasing productivity by reducing prices. In my view the advantages of increased productivity should not accrue solely to the owners and the employees but to the consumers as well.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
removal of the sales tax on production machinery and equipment as a further inducement to defer capital spending.
We made clear it was the purpose of these measures to slow down the rate of increase of business and consumer expenditure, stretch out our prosperity and sustain our economic growth. These measures were clearly of the right kind. They have worked. They have been approved in Canada and elsewhere, recently, for example by the authoritative Federal Reserve Bank of New York which commented:
Canada has clearly made a major effort to adapt general monetary and fiscal policy to the requirements of a strongly stimulated economy and has, in the process, broken new ground in the development of flexibility in fiscal policy.
I should like to say that had our example been followed elsewhere I think the world would not be suffering inflationary pressure quite as strong as it is.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is now evident, however, that the total effect of our monetary and fiscal measures has not been enough to keep the total increase in the demands on the economy down to the objectives set in the budget. I think the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada has been well conceived and skillfully applied, despite the very difficult circumstances with which it has had to cope. But I think that we in Canada, and other countries as well, have left too much to be done by monetary policy. This has resulted in conditions in the capital and money markets which are now so difficult and abnormal that they may impede the smooth and efficient flow of savings into productive investment. A larger flow of savings would help to meet the situation.
Savings are a most important aspect of the fight against inflation. Canadians, either as individuals or through corporations, lay aside a good proportion of their earnings for future use. We are one of the countries of the world which save a high proportion of their income. Our over-all rate of savings compares well from year to year with many other countries. In this present situation an increase in corporate and individual rates of savings would serve both to moderate the level of demand and to reduce the pressure in capital markets, and as one means of encouraging individuals to save we shall shortly be offering a special centennial issue of Canada savings bonds. I expect the announcement to be made in a few days.

It is clear, Mr. Chairman, that we should strengthen our fiscal policy so that it can carry a greater share of the load of restraining the excessive growth in demand now taking place. Ordinary budget considerations lead to this conclusion as well as the present economic circumstances.
In the budget in March, after taking into account the tax changes then proposed, I anticipated budgetary revenues this year of $8,300 million, excluding the yield of the refundable tax. Our budgetary expenditures I forecast at $8,450 million. This left a budgetary deficit of $150 million. In terms of the national economic accounts I forecast a surplus of some $650 million including the refundable tax yield.
That was a budget designed to restrain inflation. That is why I have no hesitation in saying it was the right kind of budget, and I am sorry it did not work as well as we all hoped it would for reasons which have emerged since the budget. In fact, I recall in the debate which took place on that occasion some members wondered in the spring of this year whether we were going to be faced with inflation or recession. The government certainly had no doubt. I certainly had no doubt, and I am happy to say we did bring in that kind of budget.	,
Our latest estimate for our revenues this fiscal year shows them at approximately the same level as forecast in the budget. The yields of some items such as corporation income tax are down slightly below the forecast, while others are up enough to offset these.
On the expenditure side it is harder to make a revised forecast at this stage until we know the timing of some of the changes that are under way. Parliament has not yet decided, for example, on what date the income guarantee program, announced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in July, will come into effect. This is one of the unknowns.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Has the government decided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and parliament has yet to decide, but the government has its plans. These will be announced in due course, and there is no intention of changing anything about that.
As is now widely known, we will have to face some increases in pay for the armed services, and I should add in veterans' disability pensions and veterans' allowances. It is
September 8, 1966

too early to forecast just what these will mean in this current year. I would think, however, it would be prudent to anticipate a total of $8,600 million in budgetary expenditures quite apart from the income guarantee program. Consequently we now anticipate a budget deficit of about $300 million and a corresponding reduction in the surplus on the national economic accounts basis.
The development in the economic situation since the time of the budget indicates the need for a stronger fiscal policy, taking into account what I have said about excessive reliance on monetary policy. May I say in this connection that this is a complaint that is equally applicable in many other countries of the world, particularly in North America. In the United States monetary conditions are even tighter than they are in Canada, and the President of the United States and the Secretary of the Treasury have, like myself, admitted that there has been too great reliance on monetary policy.
It was indicated in July that revenue measures would have to be considered to meet the burden of the income guarantee program. I have reached the conclusion that when this program is enacted it will be necessary to increase taxes or to introduce new taxes to meet our total requirements and to prevent the government's own increasing expenditures from having inflationary effects.
When we have before us, perhaps in late October, the measures to authorize the increased revenues made necessary by the income guarantee plan we will be able to review our general fiscal position and consider what changes are desirable in the light of the economic and financial situation. Until that time I will not endeavour to be more precise as to magnitudes nor announce any decision as to the nature of the measures that would be most appropriate. Needless to say, one can never anticipate tax changes.
In order to keep future tax increases to a minimum and still contain the inflationary pressures, the government has decided that it must moderate the rate of increase in expenditures, deferring some programs already planned, terminating others, and putting restrictions on still others. We are having a long and painful review of these expenditure programs with this in mind.
One of the decisions taken was to discontinue the winter housebuilding incentive program, which now does not appear to us as necessary since the same effects in regard to the volume of construction in the winter can
23033-520J
Supply-Finance
be obtained through suitable control of the direct lending by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
While the government is strongly in favour of increasing grants for research as a basic long-term policy, we will have to exercise more restraint in the rate of increase this year than we had hoped would be necessary.
The scholarship program which it had been our original intention to introduce this year will be deferred. I think the essential needs at present can be met from our student loan program on the one hand and the extensive provincial student aid programs on the other hand.
The agreements with the provinces for support of certain forestry programs expire next March and we have decided they should not be renewed as we feel the provinces are quite able to carry on themselves.
We are seeking to hold down the size of the defence budget despite the inescapable increases in pay and in the prices of what we have to buy. We shall continue to restrict our capital expenditures although this will mean some slowing down in a number of desirable programs and a postponement of good projects. I noticed the recognition of some hon. members opposite that many good projects may have to be deferred, and that is why I said this has been a painful review, very painful, and even after we have made all the changes that will be made there is still bound to be a substantial increase in government expenditures.
We have decided that we must defer the commencement of one major program that is already before the house. Many of the provincial governments have indicated that they feel we are attributing too much urgency to the introduction of full medicare programs right away, and they do not feel prepared to proceed to put such programs into effect next summer as provided for in the bill before the house. We therefore propose to defer the effective date of the plan for a year until July 1, 1968. The legislation will be proceeded with in the house as a high priority item when we reassemble at the beginning of October. The government has no intention of changing the substance of the bill other than its effective date.
Obviously this decision on medicare was a difficult one for this government to make because we have been, and remain, so strongly in favour of this major social reform. We feel, however, that the delay will help to meet the immediate financial problems of

September 8, 1366
Supply-Finance
both the federal and provincial governments and contribute to the ultimate success of the program.
The provinces and the municipalities have been increasing their expenditures as well as the federal government, including of course their very large expenditures on education. They face just as great demands as we do for increased services and facilities, and they have been sharing with us the unpleasant necessity of increasing taxes. It is certainly desirable that we and the provincial governments should harmonize our policies in expenditures, as in fiscal policies generally, taking due account of priorities and economic circumstances.
I shall of course be discussing these matters and others with provincial representatives in the tax structure committee next week. The provinces have made clear that they need and want more revenue and would like us to reduce our taxes so that they can increase theirs, as we have done for a number of years past. Our present economic situation and our foreseeable federal financial position do not permit such action on our part now. Discussions of our problems and policies as well as the general fiscal and economic outlook are necessary before we all make our plans for next year, to be submitted to parliament and the legislatures, including the main fiscal arrangements between us for the five years commencing in 1967.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It is to our fiscal policy therefore that we must look for some further assistance in restraining during this boom period the excessive total demands upon the economy that are currently making possible and in part bringing about the increases in costs and prices that are causing concern to hon. members and to very many Canadians. This is not an easy answer nor a very welcome one to those of us who must take action to cut back expenditures or increase taxes. Higher taxes are cold comfort to those troubled by higher prices, but they can help prevent prices going up more and more. I can assure the house that if higher taxes are necessary they will be proposed with a careful concern for ability to pay.
Measures such as these are, nevertheless, a relatively small cost to pay for the continuation of an expanding Canada-to avoid the grim alternative of boom and bust. We who have the responsibility of government intend to face up to the task confident that we shall

have the support of parliament and of the Canadian people.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just before sitting down, Mr. Chairman, may I indicate the measures President Johnson has announced today which have a familiar ring. He has proposed in a five point program a temporary suspension of the tax credit which permits firms to deduct from their tax bills up to 7 per cent of the funds spent on plant expansion and modernization and a six month suspension of laws permitting corporations to benefit from an accelerated depreciation program. These are very similar to the measures we took earlier this year in the budget. He also proposes that he would carefully review appropriation bills clearing Congress and establish priorities to see what could be impounded, postponed and stretched out. I could not give a better description of what I have been saying today. This is a necessary condition and one which is to be found in the United Kingdom. I hope we never will have to emulate the British course here. It was necessary there because they were unable to contain their inflationary pressures soon enough. If we keep ourselves expanding in accord with our physical possibilities, I think we can avoid stop and go. All it requires is a little sense and some restraint.
The President also proposed that Treasury Secretary Fowler would conduct a survey to determine what federal securities should be withheld from the already tight money market. Finally, he would ask the Federal Reserve Board in the light of the other actions to move to help bring down soaring interest rates. I should like to add that if the kind of measures I am proposing today are implemented I think this will help bring down interest rates.

Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?
Progress reported.

Mr. Chairman, when it came to my attention that I was to lead off for the opposition on this item I began to put down the observations that I wished to make in the time allotted to me. The first thought that
Supply-Finance
flashed through my mind was: Never had a speaker, on the opening estimates of the Department of Finance, so many targets. It reminds me of a time during the depression when the rabbit population got very thick on the prairies and many of us went out to reduce that population somewhat, partially for sport and partially for food. As the owls chased the rabbits in from the fields toward the bluffs and the trees on the farm you could fire your rifle as fast as you were able, and they still kept coming in waves.
That is the way this government has been functioning for three and a half years: No matter how many mistakes they have made, they keep coming in waves with more-and the mistake that I think is inherent in the minister's statement this afternoon will probably be one more and one of the most serious. It has been said that to be minister of finance is the graveyard of politicians who have ambition.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Also national defence.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Well, you survived.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
The remarks made by the minister this afternoon put him very deep in the six-foot hole that is customary in graveyards. In my judgment the speech this afternoon was a complete victory for the establishment. The same establishment that we met up with when we were the government has now won a complete victory.
Let me remind the committee that one of the great stories that has to be told is that in 1945, following the war, Canada was faced with inflationary pressures and the civil servants of that day had to meet them. In the Korean war there was another inflationary period, and the civil servants of that day had to help meet it. Then we had a period of the great influx of capital into our country from 1953 to 1955. This was an altogether different type of inflationary pressure-and the civil service had to help the government meet it.
These three great crises in the financial aspects of running a government so thoroughly penetrated the thinking of those who advise the government on financial matters both fiscal and monetary that they lived in everlasting fear of inflationary pressures. When we were the government we faced two recessions, in 1957-58 and again in 1961. Even when we were facing recessions we had advice poured on us to take anti-inflationary measures. The worst feature of this situation was that the person who was the spokesman and had control over the monetary policy was

Supply-Finance
going one way, with a tight money policy, and the government formed of the elected representatives of the people of this country was going the other way. We finally resolved that difficulty by the dismissal of the governor of the Bank of Canada.
