speechtext:
Our government was included, and so was yours, because we were both part of the end product being produced in this country by the financial establishment. This group is so able, so sincere and so dedicated that they find it very easy to persuade themselves that they know how to run the country better than the elected representatives of the people.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
This is what the statement of the minister means tonight, that he has completely accepted their point of view. He has accepted a series of techniques of dealing with financial measures which are as old and as orthodox as financial measures both fiscal and monetary could be. This is simply a retreat into techniques that have not worked in the past, that have destroyed governments and that will destroy this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: And that have brought about the most prosperous conditions this country has ever seen.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
The government today is living in the most prosperous conditions this country has ever known and which were brought about in 1961. Every action of the government since it came to power in 1963 has led to the conditions in which we find ourselves today. Let no one think this happened since the last budget. Let your mind go

back to the last three and a half years. In the fall of 1962, with a minority government just elected continuing the expansion program of the previous two years, the leader of the opposition, who is now the Prime Minister of Canada, announced on several occasions in the month of September that he considered it his duty to stop anything going through this house and to force the government of that time to its knees.
That is the start of the policy for which the minister is paying a price tonight. We were able to pass no estimates and no legislation. The wealthy and the "wise" of this country got together to destroy us; but now the minister has put himself in the hands of those who destroyed us. The result of that will be that he and his government will face the same fate. That is the significance of his remarks tonight. This is the victory of the old fashioned techniques of bringing in measures too late and increasing the possibilities of a recession in 1967. Everyone knows that for the last two years our Canadian economy, because of the drive we started in 1961 toward expansion at home and abroad, has been walking on a tightrope, a tightrope between recession on one hand and inflation on the other.
This is not a new subject, Mr. Chairman, and I intend to deal with what has been said by those of us on this side of the house concerning this matter. However, before I get into the actual facts respecting a situation which is very serious, and will have negative results for the future of Canada, let us look at the members of the cabinet. Anyone with half an eye can see that there is something drastic disturbing them. I saw the Minister of National Health and Welfare-

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Where is he?

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
Running around with a tight face. I knew immediately that there was something wrong. I know when a man walks through Gethsemane; I know he appealed to one man and another of his colleagues because the government was in crisis again. And where is the minister tonight? He has been destroyed by the cabal which is temporarily in control in the cabinet. I have watched the ministers being destroyed one after another in the last three and a half years, as different groups in the party fought each other. I saw the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the new minister of manpower, one of the most promising men to
September 8. 19B6

have come up from French speaking Canada in recent years, led to the slaughter on the railway strike bill, sacrificed on the altar. I have seen these men betrayed and the rug pulled from under them.
This is a divided government, one that has always been divided. They do not worry any more about crises cropping up once a year or once a month; now they worry about them every minute. This is a divided cabinet, which has to go.
Let us look at all the other measures which will be cut down, ones that the traditional type of finance minister thinks of cutting first, such as the $500 to try and even out the flow of employment in the construction of domestic homes in winter. Research is another victim, although it is certainly one of the things that would cause a reduction of inflationary pressures. Education, a longterm solution to inflation in any country, is also to get the axe. Forestry, at a time when forestry products in the northern hemisphere, are in the greatest demand, is to be curtailed. I will not say a thing about defence. It has already been indicated that instead of maintaining an army to defend this country and to bear our share in the defence of North America, we are now establishing a police force armed w_th police billies instead of rifles. Capital expenses will be cut down.
That brings me to the question of the old fashioned technique of cutting down what is vulnerable, such as, for instance, medicare. A year ago I said in this house that any person who tries to pretend to the people of Canada that medicare will be put into effect in Canada by July 1, 1967 is only fooling the people. And yet we have witnessed a great campaign through the press, radio, through pamphlets and managed news in the magazines that medicare will bring an end to all our problems, that every ache and pain will be over on July 1, 1967. This was backed by a pledge of the minister who was allowed to make that pledge. The truth has now come home, and another minister is biting the dust. The provinces have been led to believe that with the Liberal party in power all will be well. Next week the axe will fall on them also.
Today we heard the minister telling us, in smug terms of the statement made by President Johnson in the United States. We would be better off if the government would stop thinking about the United States and trying to keep in step with that country. We must realize that the same bunch of people in
Supply-Finance
the United States are cosy with a similar bunch of people in Canada. You cannot tell the difference between their policies on defence and fiscal matters, and our policies. They are good, sincere and able men, but their minds are fixed on the past. They will not listen and let the fresh air of new ideas come into their thoughts. They destroyed us and they will destroy this government.
Last night I listened with interest to the minister's speech on television. He tried to blame everyone but the government for inflation.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Who is to blame for this inflation, the opposition? He says the bad boys of the N.D.P. are pushing us too fast. He says these bad boys in the Conservative party push us too fast. He says the opposition is to blame. Who took the attitude that all democratic government would stop in the fall of 1962? The present Prime Minister took that attitude. He had a group of devoted people behind him who stopped everything we tried to do from this side of the house in the fall of 1962. Who brought in the budget in 1963, the opposition? Then, we had 60 days of decision. That budget was a restrictive budget. That budget inferred all the th'ngs the royal commission had intimated in 1957, and Mr. Gordon undertook to put into it the ideas set out in "Troubled Canada" as well as the restrictive ideas developed at the Kingston conference.
All these higher taxes were part of the 60 days of decision. Who started the 11 per cent tax on production machinery that added to the costs at the very root of all costs? If 1 remember accurately all the parties in the opposition condemned the government for adding on that 11 per cent tax. However the government believed in restrictions. This was their name for planning. The establishment was in control. Well, we got a few of the restrictions removed, but it was not the opposition that put on the taxes or put on the restrictions.
Then, let us jump ahead to the budget of 1965. I spoke during that debate and I have a copy of my speech here. This was a year and a half ago, Mr. Chairman, and I warned the government then about what was happening. The present member for Davenport was then the minister of finance. He said that we were going to have an inflationary budget to get this country going, but he was going to an election. So, we have this silly situation, with

September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
inflation beginning to show signs of gathering momentum in 1965 and a finance minister thinking in terms of one thing only, namely getting the Liberals back into power with a majority. I have the record here and I intend to quote from it. However, I should like to remind the committee that this is not only my view. I just happened to be reading an article in Time magazine a few months ago. This article is dated June 3, 1966, and the subject is "The Realm of Canada". The part I should like to quote is under the heading, "Everything but Business", and states:
Gallup's conclusion that the "Munsinger affair did considerable harm to the image" of the P.M. was something of a surprise, considering that the Liberals intended it to cut the other way. Obviously, the answers were weighted by the universal assumption that Pearson will not contest another election. But the Gallup poll also failed to note that the mood was as much inspired by a series of earlier irritations. First there was the budget blight of 1963, then the flag argument of 1964, followed by last year's Rivard affair, and penultimately the sticky business of postal clerk spy George Victor Spencer earlier this year. The fact that Pearson personally telephoned Spencer to ask if the spy wanted a judicial inquiry was not the first instance of the P.M.'s diplomatic instinct leading him politically astray, but possibly it was the worst example of his unnecessary dabbling in dirt. Munsinger was too much. "More than anything else," suggested a Toronto Liberal last week of Pearson's diminished public support, "it's just an accumulation of everything but doing the nation's business."
This is the charge I level at the government tonight. They have time for "Bi and Bi" commissions; they have time for debates on capital punishment; they have time for flag debates. All these things have merit, but the government has no time for the nation's business. This government has been so busy carrying on elections that they have no time for anything else. The 1963 election was unnecessary, and the one in 1965 was doubly unnecessary. Now, as a result of the sheer weakness of their position, we are stumbling into another one in 1966. This government has been so busy trying to get a majority so they will have complete control of the country, as they believe, that they have no time to govern. We are paying for their sins now.
In the time that is left to me, I want to deal, and I can only do so in very elementary form, with the fact that there are long-term solutions to inflation, and short-term solutions to inflation, as the minister stated. No one quarrels with the desire to find out more about an income policy. No one quarrels with any of these long-range objectives which we all have. The problem as I pointed out in

1965 and again in 1966 in my budget speeches, is one of finding short-range solutions. This country today is even more precariously balanced on the tightrope than it was five months ago. Five months ago I proposed, in essence, that the answer was not a whole series of anti-inflationary measures, just as the answer was not a whole series of inflationary measures. The obsolete proposals for coping with these problems are all on file in the offices of this government, available for every minister; but is it not about time we began to use the knowledge we have and to realize that today there are some forces in Canada that are deflationary, just as there were a year and a half ago? These deflationary forces are there. Likewise there are pressure points for inflation.
Budget making now in 1966 is not the same as it was in the days of the horse and buggy or in 1867. I suggested that we should have a series of short-range proposals, some of which were anti-inflationary and some of which were expansionist. These things work against each other, and would keep us balanced on the tightrope until we got through this pressure period. Without going into great detail, I will start with the budget of 1965, and some of my statements. I quote:
Now, Mr. Speaker, this budget adds another inflationary force by trying to increase consumer spending. Second, there is a shortage of skilled labour in almost every line of activity, and this produces a cost-push inflation . . .
Third, there is a tremendous need for new capital for plant expansion . . . Why is the government not aware of them?
I put forward three propositions and asked why the government was not aware of them. I did not know they were planning an election; I was simply trying to be constructive. I dealt with this 11 per cent tax and said that this was at the root of a lot of our trouble. Then I quoted from a document published by the Economic Council and proceeded to outline 17 or 18 proposals, mostly short-range, which would help the government ease away from this inflationary pressure. They are all there-one, two, three, four, five, six, and right down to 14. I was trying to be constructive.
This year, I was even more precise because I saw the situation more clearly. Let me quote just a few paragraphs from what I said on April 1, 1966, as recorded at page 3751 of Hansard:
9 (7:30 p.m.)
If the previous minister of finance was following nationalistic policies that are 60 years out of date,
September 8, 1966

I think it can be said of the present Minister of Finance that he is only 25 years out of date.
I change that now and I say that they are both 60 years out of date. I went on:
Last year the minister supported his predecessor's proposals. Last year the minister and his predecessor ignored the clear and present warnings which we on this side of the house gave about inflation. Last year the Minister of Finance indicated that he would stand or fall with his colleague. This year I think one can say he has done nothing in particular, and has done it very well.
Then I went on and talked about the fundamental problems that we had been talking about, and I said:
The tragedy of this budget, Mr. Speaker, is that the minister has not faced up to the fundamental decision which confronts Canada, and that is how to utilize the human and material resources of Canada so that the economy can operate closer to its essential capacity.
Then I proceeded in a series of positive suggestions to pick out those areas, and I can summarize them in this way. First of all there was the principle of selectivity. In some areas you should force expansion by offering incentives. These areas embrace the steel industry, the petrochemical industry, and so on. Then there are areas where you should check expansion-for example the construction industry-by selection of your fiscal program to meet the needs in each of the industrial segments. This is one positive approach which has never been utilized in this country.
Second, I made a big pitch for a temporary manpower policy. Instead of waiting for all of these long-range solutions of the minister of manpower, we should get right down to the facts. We have thousands of able people who are willing to help but are not being given the chance. I would point out that only 34 per cent of our women between the ages of 21 and 45 are in the work force. This is the lowest percentage in the world of women in this age group who are working.
Our women are just as able to meet a national emergency as any other group in the country, but there is no leadership. We have great numbers of people who are retired at 55, 60 and 65 and who are at the peak of their mental capacity, and they are willing to be called on a temporary basis back to the working force. We do not have to wait a year or two for them; they will go back to work in two weeks. If the government would say what their policy is, the manufacturers, the hospitals and all the other people who need help will get them back to work. It can be done very simply on a fiscal incentive basis which is not inflationary, but will get at one
Supply-Finance
of the basic causes, namely labour shortages in certain segments of the economy.
The third point that I made last April was that no one has looked seriously at the various ways of meeting inflation on the monetary side The minister was quite right today when he said that we put too much faith in the monetary capacity of the Bank of Canada to settle this question. The bank has only a marginal impact. What it is, no one knows-20 per cent, 30 per cent; I do not know. But when you put the millions of little people in this country on your side, they know all about the high cost of meat and the high cost of everything which they buy, and they are willing now to co-operate with you. You can kill two birds with one stone by using the little people of this country, who have only a few dollars a month, to help the situation out. If they knew they would get their money back, they would be much more willing to put it aside.
What does the minister imply today? The old-fashioned technique of taxing the people and taking their money away by that method. And I have not mentioned the worst aspect. If the government want to clear the pressure on capital spending, there is one move they can make. Under the Canada Pension Plan the government will take $400 million a year out of the people of this country, which represents 3.6 per cent of the labour payroll. The government turns this $400 million over to the provinces.

Let the government go back to their original plan if they like. Mr. Lesage has gone; he cannot stop you now. The government does not have to make a backroom deal with Mr. Johnson. The workingman has only been assessed this amount of deduction during the last few months. Half of 3.6 is 1.8. Can you blame the labour union leaders for asking for more when the pay of the workers keeps going down? Who started this inflation? The government who started it had high hopes, but they fell flat on their faces as they made deals with Lesage which hurt this country,

September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
and which are hurting it more than anything else at the present time.
Let us turn the people loose, because they want to help. They want to cut their costs and they are quite willing to go out and work. They are not going to stay in the labour force once the emergency is over in the next two or three years; they will be glad to go back home. But give them the incentive to work. This is what I call a peaking policy. Give the little people of the country the chance to save, and in such a way that they know that by saving they are going to reduce the cost of the things that they buy, and that they are going to get their money back with increased increments when the time comes.
I could go on and list suggestion after suggestion, but I will not. All I will do is to plead with the minister that, as he prepares his baby budget this fall, that he break clear from these reactionary right-wing, obsolete methods of the last century. I ask him to give some of the new thoughts an opportunity to be tried out. This country is not going to collapse. We are strong; we are just beginning to get up speed. Our railways need to expand and our steel industry needs to expand. The government should back that expansion, and at the same time put the antiinflationary forces to work to balance that expansion. I ask the government to give us some leadership. If they do, I am sure they will be surprised at how the people will respond and follow the leadership of 20th century thinking. But they cannot help but be disillusioned by leadership under the hand of a reactionary group of the old guard on 'fiscal and monetary matters who draw their inspiration from the 19th century.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it would not be quite true to say that I was surprised at the statement of the minister this afternoon. I did not expect very much, though I must say that I was somewhat surprised at the lengths to which he went in promoting extremely orthodox views, not to say reactionary views. I do not intend to deal with his statement yet because I have some quite positive suggestions to make to which I hope the minister will listen with some attention.
The only comment that I want to make on his speech at the moment is to remark on the airy assumption that he made, without the slightest supporting evidence, that we are inclined to do too many things in Canada at the same time; that we have reached the
(Mr. Hamilton.]
limit of our productivity. There is no evidence at all to support that statement and, on the other hand, there has been no examination of how our resources are being used at the present time.
The minister makes this statement in light of a report from the Economic Council of Canada that per capita productivity in Canada is 23 per cent less than it is in the United States. I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that unless we are prepared to accept the idea that Canadian workmen are less competent, less efficient and lazier than those of the United States, this would indicate to me that there is something radically wrong with the structuring of our industrial society.
This question of inflation, of the rise in the cost of living, cannot be fruitfully considered in isolation or dealt with in the way the minister proposes-by monetary and fiscal measures divorced from the general economic picture.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Primarily it must be considered in terms of our actual and potential productivity, to determine whether or not we really have actual and runaway inflation which can be cured only by drastic monetary and fiscal measures, and whether in fact the situation conforms to the classical definition of too much money chasing too few goods.
We must examine our whole industrial and financial machinery to determine how well it is succeeding in using our human and material resources to produce the maximum in goods and services for the Canadian people. On the face of it, one must view with considerable suspicion the contention that Canada has reached its limit in this regard. I, for one, find it an insult to my intelligence to be told that 20 million people with an exceptionally high level of technical skill, in possession of the world's largest per capita store of unexploited natural resources, are not capable of producing goods and services to satisfy their demands. Yet, this is what the minister says. This is what we are told when terms such as "an overheated economy" are used to describe a society which, owning enormous real and potential wealth, yet suffers slums, housing shortages, inadequate educational and health services and, I might say, a barbarical-ly low cultural level to exist within its boundaries.
I think it is time perhaps that we kicked this bogeyman of runaway inflation, this
September 8, 1968



scarecrow that is held up to frighten us, out of the way, and took a hard look at the institutions and arrangements which link our economy with the rest of the world-the institutions and arrangements by which we produce wealth from our enormous natural resources. For one thing I think we should take a look at our tariff structure. It has something to do with our link with the rest of the world. First of all we must examine our own internal legal and institutional arrangements to see how well or ill they contribute to the goal of maximum production. We are again being offered all the old moss-grown explanations for the rise in the cost of living. Faced with steadily rising prices, the consumer is being persuaded to place the blame on labour, and in some instances, on the farmer. Labour is accused of exorbitant demands which increase costs, with the added suggestion that the Canadian worker does not work hard enough to justify his demands. The farmer is accused of inefficiency and of failure to keep up with the times.
With regard to the charge against labour, there has been a continuing battle of the statisticians and economists. One can prove anything by carefully selected statistics and I do not propose to enter into the battle, which in many cases tends to be one between special pleaders. I have no hesitation in saying that anyone who has worked as it is possible that some of us have, in Canadian industrial plants, or who cares to enter and observe the operations in a Canadian factory will be unable to leave that factory convinced that the Canadian worker does not work hard and efficiently with the means placed at his disposal by his employer. Furthermore, no fair-minded person, on examining the wage scale of the Canadian working force will be able, in good conscience, to contend that the Canadian working force draws an undue share of the wealth which it produces. The charge against labour is in essence a demand of other and more fortunate sections of the community to continue to enjoy a privileged position in our midst.
The charge against the farmer is, if anything, even more ill founded than the charge against labour. In no section of our economy has the impact of modern technology been so great as it has been in the agricultural sector, with the consequent result that efficiency and productivity have been increased. The proof of this is to be found in the enormously increased agricultural production, coupled
Supply-Finance
with the dramatic decline in farm population. If the farmer is to be blamed for anything, it is for his failure to combine with his fellow farmers, to ensure the distribution of agricultural products to the consumer at prices that will be fair to himself and to the consumer.
It is too easy, too simplistic to find the cause of the continual rise in the cost of living in the greed and indolence of labour, and in the stupidity of the farmer. These are myths without foundation in fact, and we must dig deeper to find the real causes.
From time to time, Mr. Chairman, faced with the rapacity of the free enterprise system, legislators and parliaments have enacted legislation in an attempt to cope with the more rapacious aspects of the acquisitive society. In the course of time such legislation, without regard to its effectiveness in the public interest, has come to assume the position of a sacred cow, taking its place in the pantheon of the good, along with motherhood, marriage, thrift, and piety. One such sacred cow has been the Combines Investigation Act, and I am well aware that when I propose, as I am about to do, that we scrap this legislation, I shall run the risk of being charged with hardly less than sacrilege. If we look this sacred cow firmly in her soft brown eye, we shall find she is what dairy farmers call a "boarder"-a cow that looks nice but provides no butterfat.
In the first place this act is ineffectual. It would be difficult, and perhaps impossible, to cite a single instance in which an action under the Combines Investigation Act has proven successful in preventing collusion to act in concert by businesses which are supposed to be, ostensibly, in competition.
Even more difficult to be proved would be the contention that a success in preventing such collusion would have been in the public interest. The truth is that the developments which the act was designed to frustrate are developments inevitable and necessary in an industrial society-the growth of units of production of a magnitude great enough to be capable of the most economical and efficient use of human and material resources-a magnitude which will vary from industry to industry, and from period to period.
This is not to say, Mr. Chairman, that the large enterprises necessary to modern production do not place in hands of their owners and managers enormous power to levy an unconscionable tribute on the public. Other means than the prevention of this development must be found to curb the misuse of

suggested that he now agrees with us -though he did not agree with us some months ago-that he has been relying too much on monetary control and not enough on fiscal policy. But even his attempt to use monetary policy has been based, I suggest, on at least one big fallacy. I suggest to the minister that contrary to the conventional wisdom that high interest rates have a deflationary effect and act to cool down an overheated economy, any real examination of their effect in the present stage of our economy must lead to the opposite conclusion.
In the first place, directly or indirectly, interest enters into every cost and as it is inevitably passed along to the end of the line where the consumer stands, it must have the effect of increasing prices. The argument that high interest rates tend to cut down consumption is simply not borne out by the facts. The businessman will not be deterred by high interest rates, so long as a booming full employment economy exists. He will be confident of being able to pass it along the line.
Evidence before the banking and commerce committee in 1955 or 1956 proved that the client of the small loan companies is not only not deterred by high interest rates but does not even bother to find out what he is paying. The terms of repayment are his only concern. If the monthly payment seems within his means he has little care about the rate. As for slowing down the investment rate it is obvious that interest rates are of marginal importance in an economy in which over 70 per cent of all investment comes from internally generated savings. High rates encourage the inflow of foreign capital and in the final analysis merely increase costs and raise prices. For these reasons we suggest that to prevent a general rise in interest rates, with its inflationary results, the government should take action to prevent such a rise by using the powers conferred on it by the British North America Act. This would not only control the inflationary effect of high interest rates but would enable the government to take steps to allocate credit to areas which might otherwise be starved, such as housing, and enable us to set some social goals.
Earlier this afternoon the minister told us that the government was seeking to curb inflationary measures by cutting down public expenditure. He went on to say that he was using persuasion with those in the private sector of our economy. I can tell him that in my part of the country his persuasion does not seem to have had very much effect. On
Supply-Finance
the outskirts of the small town in which I live on Vancouver island, two enormous shopping centre complexes are being built at the present moment, one of them costing over $11 million. We already have five shopping centres in the area. Evidently, the minister was not able to persuade these people to defer their expenditures. He preferred, rather, to cut down on the expenditures of government-to take the position that those who own and control supermarkets can spend anything they like, but that Canadians acting in concert to develop amenities for their own purposes must not be allowed to do so. I think the minister had better take a correspondence course in persuasion, since his efforts have obviously had no effect whatsoever on those who control the private sector of the economy.
I would hate to be a Liberal tonight. It will be very difficult for them. But I have a suggestion I should like to pass on to the minister-it came from one of my colleagues. He suggested that since we are not to have medicare now, why not postpone it until 1969 and make it a nice, round, half-century since the minister's party first promised it to the people of Canada.
I have tried to place the question of inflation and the rising cost of living within the total framework of our economic possibilities in Canada. I wish now to place it within an even wider context. There has been a long continuing	debate-perhaps	"muttering"
might be a better word-among certain hon. gentlemen opposite and I take it that the present Minister of Finance is on one side of this debate, or muttering, and that the former Minister of Finance is on the other. It is a debate between nationalism and continental-ism. There are those on one side who tell us that as next door neighbours to the United States, as those who share this rich North American continent with the United States, we must adjust ourselves and our economy to the necessities of continentalism even at the expense of our national identity.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Then we have those on the other side who suggest to us that while it is true there are a great many benefits to receive from being part of the North American industrial and economic complex, we must preserve our national identity even at the cost of relinquishing many of the advantages that might come to us through continentalism.
It seems to me that this is too simplistic, too black and white, too much the concept of

September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
either or. I suggest to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that if he will just proceed with policies that will assist our industrial productivity potential, and at the same time not allow the private sector to waste resources, if he will take positive steps to curb that tendency, then we can hope to lay the foundations of a policy which will enable us to gain the benefits, and they are undoubtedly tremendous benefits, that accrue from being part of the North American continent, next door neighbours to the richest and wealthiest nation in the history of the world.
But we are not going to do this as long as our Minister of Finance sits back and, without a shred of evidence, tells us that we have reached the limit of our productive capacities, that we must not expect to go on as we have been doing, and yet at the same time we have only to look around the private sector and see the gross extravagance and misuse of resources. In this situation the minister relies on persuasion to get them to stop doing these nasty things, and they pay no attention to the minister, just as I would not if I were in their shoes. I would only pay attention to a minister who is decisive enough to say, "This is a control that is going in and it is going to have the force of law; and that is that."

It was not exactly a financial collapse; but what I am afraid of is that we are going to have a social collapse in this country.
I would like the minister to examine the propositions I have put before him tonight, to ask himself very seriously whether he has made any examination of the structuring of our industrial economy, and whether he has any evidence that we have reached the ultimate in our progress because, if he has not, then he has no right to come before the representatives of the Canadian people and tell them the Canadian people are too lazy, too stupid and too dishonest to take advantage of their unexampled opportunities as inhabitants of one of the richest countries in the world.
I hope the minister will consider this. I hope that the violent reactions he is going to get from his reactionary speech tonight will make him realize that the government in dealing with inflation must not rely on sudden, ad hoc, violent fiscal and monetary policies because they won't work, but must seriously examine the whole structure of our society and decide what steps the government can take to rationalize it, to increase its productivity and to lay the basis for a wealthy society that no longer will need to tolerate slums, poverty, deficient education, deficient health services, and all the things of which every decent Canadian is ashamed of today. I hope the minister is not so sunk in his 19th century orthodoxy that he will refuse to look at these things.
I shall conclude by telling the minister this incident. When he was speaking in the house in the debate on the Bank Act I had a friend here from a foreign country who, to my mind, was not particularly progressive or leftist. He listened to the Minister of Finance and when I went to collect him from the gallery and we were walking along the corridor he said to me, "But, but, but I don't understand. Your minister comes right out of the 19th century. How can you have any planification"? I said, "My dear man, we have no planification because our minister and government do come straight out of the 19th century". Mr. Chairman, I suggest they try to move into the 20th century before the last part of it disappears.

Mr. Chairman, we listened closely to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) this afternoon when he informed us of the government's plans to meet the financial conditions now prevailing in Canada.
In order to check inflation and try to prevent economic chaos, the minister proposed this afternoon certain measures which will require further sacrifices from the Canadian people, and mean, in a word, that they will have to tighten their belts once again in order to avoid the worst. It is always the same old story year after year; the Canadian people are asked to make sacrifices, to do without such and such a thing in order to establish an economic balance according to the requirements of the monetary and fiscal system existing in our country.
The minister said this afternoon:
We have had a long and strong economic expansion in the past five and a half years. It has carried us from a condition of serious and persistent unemployment to one of widespread prosperity and virtually full employment. There is still too much unemployment in certain areas of Canada, and among those who are poorly educated and unskilled but this arises from reasons other than a shortage of opportunities in Canada taken as a whole.
It is no doubt because there is no shortage of opportunities that workers are transferred from one place to another, 1000, 1500 or 2000 miles apart.
And he added:
Total expenditures of money by consumers, by business, by government-and by those who want our exports-are now more than adequate to support a healthy level of economic growth.
The minister admits that the demand is more than adequate to support a healthy level of economic growth.
But he contradicts himself. The government has been in contradiction since it came to power. Last week, we were considering two bills: Bill C-230 to provide for the resumption of operations by the railway workers by granting them an increase of 18 per cent in wages. At the same time, we were being presented with bill C-231, to authorize in proud terms, the railways to increase their freight rates, which will obviously bring about a further increase in the cost of living. The government asked us to pass the two bills last week and, this week, the Minister
Supply

Finance
of Finance (Mr. Sharp) keeps on repeating
his gospel:
Speaking generally, Canadians have been very impatient to get on with very many things both directly and through their governments-and now, we are paying the price of trying to do too much all at once.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know who are the economists advising the minister of Finance or the government, but it seems to me these are direct contradictions, from A to Z, from the first to the last page of the epistle which the Minister of Finance presented to this house this afternoon.
The minister continued:
As a result, we have had accelerating increases in prices and costs, accompanied by urgent and pressing demands by special groups for more income, using whatever means are open to them.
At this point, the minister was alluding to the recent rail workers strike and to other strikes in every sphere of the Canadian economy.
The minister also said:
We have now reached a position that is unstable.
Last week we were in a stable position; this week we are in a position that is unstable. This reminds me of what the Liberals said in the province of Quebec during the last election campaign: For a stable government, for a stable economy, for a stable country, vote Liberal.
I see the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) is applauding; it is because this is way over his head.
Mr. Chairman, what does stability mean? According to the dictionary, the word "stable" means something that does not move, that does not go forward, nor backwards, nor sideways. This is about what we have with the present government A government which contradicts itself from week to week, ever since it took over the administration of the affairs of Canada.
And the minister adds:
The present trends just cannot continue for long into the future. We cannot all get what we want.
I would like to ask the minister's secretary to be careful about the French translation next time. Words are missing, sometimes, and it should be a perfect translation of what the minister said this afternoon. In any case, I am using the French text and here is what it says further:
We cannot get all that we want.

We cannot.
If everyone tries there is going to be an excessive rise in prices and in costs because right now the country just could not-no matter how hard it tries-produce enough to meet all the demands.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance knows that this statement is inaccurate; right now in Canada there is not a single industry which is not capable of increasing its production.
The farmers in the province of Quebec are literally starving because their production is not selling. And yet they can increase, multiply, triple, quadruple and quintuple their production as early as next year if the government will give them the assurance that their production will sell.
The minister has just told us that we cannot produce more. In the clothing industry in the province of Quebec, as well as in other provinces, plants had to close their doors because they could not sell their production. And the minister tells us that we produce everything we can.
The automobile industry, and I know what I am talking about, can increase its production as early as next year, if it is assured that its cars will sell.
In the field of farm machinery, in any field of national production in fact, our production can increase and double within a short time.
The Minister of Finance and Receiver General tells us that we cannot produce enough to meet all the demands. It is not the demand that cannot be met. Finance is to blame for +he failure to distribute goods and services in Canada to those who need them. The minister does not have the courage to cut into the monetary system, he prefers to cut into private industry, among individual Canadians who are building Canada, rather than among the financiers who are destroying and swallowing Canada.
The minister goes on to say:
Let us bear in mind some simple facts. We are now producing about all we can in Canada this year.
One more mistake and, tomorrow, all across Canada, newspapers will spread the minister's comments. But these same newspapers will shy away from reporting the comments of those who are pinpointing the real source for the "inflationary" situation in which we find ourselves at present.
Mention of this will be avoided; people will be told to tighten their belts. Why? Because
[Mr. CaouetteJ
important newspaper owners are financed in exactly the same way as the government, namely by the controllers of the economic life blood of the country, without whose permission nobody can breathe anymore. The Minister of Finance thinks he is supposed to tell the Canadian people to tighten their belts and keep from breathing for a while, for the sake of Canada's economic stability.
The Minister of Finance goes on to say that our productivity is growing by 2 or 3 per cent per year and he adds:
Our labour force is growing at a rate of a bit over three per cent a year-and is becoming better educated and trained. Our productivity-the volume of goods and services per worker that we can produce-is growing somewhere between two and three per cent a year over-all. Canadians can expect an increasing standard of living-on the average-[DOT] which increases at a rate that bears some relationship to their average increase in productivity-say about three per cent a year over a long period.
Would the minister wish to make a comparison at this stage? It results in an invitation to the workers not to demand a wage increase beyond three per cent, that is to say no greater wage increase than the increase in productivity.
Is the minister very conscientious when comes the time, for instance, to portion out the federal budget? When we see that, for the year 1966-1967, 14.9 per cent of each federal budget dollar is paid to financiers solely to cover the interest on Canada's debt. [DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Has the minister ever considered discontinuing payment of this interest over a period of "x" months, namely until Canada's economic stability has been regained? Let us discontinue payment of interests on the debt. If we ask the workers to tighten their belts, the mothers to refrain from buying what their families need, the aged not to ask for an increase of the old age pension, because that would contribute to inflation, is it not true then that the interest paid on a flictitious national debt is, in fact, contributing to inflation? A billion and a quarter, this year, in interest on the national debt alone. Why did the minister not make the statement, on an additional page which could have been page No. 10, that from now on no interest will be paid if it stems from our financial system which is strangling Canada?
If workers, families, businessmen and manufacturers are asked to make sacrifices, big financial interests should not be spared, and then the Minister of Finance will have shown courage.

There are laws to prevent business from combining to increase or maintain their prices and profits.

In 1961, there were one million unemployed in Canada; 208 Conservative members in the house could not deal with unemployment nor restore economic stability in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, this does not go back to yesterday. It is always the same, everything must always be done over again. Like the Prime Minister and like the finance minister of the former government, our economists have advised us to stop giving a $500 bonus to whoever builds a house in winter; they have told us to stop spending; our economists in the Bank of Canada have told us to do this or that. All their recommendations have tended to belittle the individual, the worker helping to build the country.
The minister continues on page 6:
I think the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada has been well conceived and skilfully applied, despite the very difficult circumstances with which it has had to cope.
Before the house adjourned in July, were we not presented with a bill to allow banks
Supply-Finance
to raise their interest rate? Was not a resolution also presented to allow chartered banks to multiply, not by 12 but by 14, their reserves in the Bank of Canada? Is the government scrupulous as to this? No. The Bank of Canada is proceeding skillfully, "despite the very difficult circumstances with which it has had to cope", and this, when the Bank of Canada does not even assume its responsibilities. Mr. Chairman, I have proof here. A short time ago, on July 21, the newspaper VAction published the following statement made in Washington by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin):
Canada made known yesterday its intention-
Mind you, "its intention"-
-of reducing the cost of money loaned to developing countries.
Let us increase the cost of money here in Canada, but let us reduce it for developing countries.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Paul Martin, speaking before the members of the O.E.C.D., said that Canada will reduce by three fourths of one per cent the administration costs applicable to low interest loans.
Low interest means that we have actually loaned money without interest to some countries, including the West Indies, to build sewers, roads and houses. Canada has loaned money. But the paradox is this: Where do we find the money to lend it to Jamaica, the West Indies and all the other countries? We borrow it at high interest rates, whereas we lend it wothout interest to developing countries. I have never seen such a stupid thing. Canada is not yet completely developed, it is still being developed, and the minister informs us that we must postpone certain government projects, in short, that we must back out of certain material projects for lack of financial means. Let us wait until later when the economic situation has improved.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs also stated:
This means that Canada's contribution to development will be interest free loans repayable over a period of 50 years, with 10 years of grace.
That means 60 years, Mr. Chairman. When Jamaica starts paying us back, the Prime Minister will have reached 130 years of age. But at the age of 130 years, he will not be here, but others will be here who may have to do then what we have done not long ago for Britain which could not pay back the $2 bill1 on; that is let them pay it back in the year 2003.

September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
Jamaica will act in just about the same way.
Mr. Chairman, it is not that I oppose the aid we are in a position to give such countries, it is only that I object to having the Minister ot Finance imposing upon us in Canada, upon people who have not enough even now, restrictions which no one thinks of imposing upon the financial system. That is revolting.
Reverting to the quotation from the article:
He spoke before the delegates of industrial nations supplying 90 per cent of foreign aid last year, which, including the communist countries last year totalled $11 billion.
That is $11 billion last year, in 1965.
As for the chairman of the World Bank, Mr. George Woods, he was highly critical yesterday of the aid given by industrial countries to developing countries. Mr. Woods stated that the amount of financial assistance to developing countries was inadequate by any reasonable standard. Since 1961, the level of net expenditures in capital funds of the O.E.C.D. member countries for underdeveloped countries has remained steady at approximately $6 billion per year, he said, and compared to the increasing revenues of O.E.C.D. countries, such expenditures have fallen from 0.8 per cent to 0.6 per cent. Exportation of private capital has increased but the major part has gone to few countries, and very little to the poorest countries.
The Chairman of the World Bank, whose statement was in strange contrast with the relative optimism shown before by the chairman of the committee, Mr. Willard Thorp, and the United States Secretary of State Mr. Dean Rusk, stated that the conditions for granting assistance tend to become more and more difficult-
That is why the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that while we were charging three quarter of one per cent for administrative costs on loans spread over periods of 50 years, with periods of grace of 10 years, there will be no more interest or administrative costs. We will pay ourselves, here in Canada, the administrative costs.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the Canadian people are being laughed at; a monetary policy is in use for foreign countries, a foreign policy definitely out of date for Canada, and the members of Parliament act as weathercocks according to statements which are an insult to the Canadian people.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Winters, said not long ago, in March 1966, as can be seen in La Presse:
Canadians should restrict their demands on the federal treasury.
Everything indicates that we can expect another year of economic progress for Canada, keeping in mind, however, that inflation remains a constant problem, said the Minister of Commerce, Mr. 
Robert Winters, speaking before the Canadian Club in Toronto.
The deficit in the balance of payments, which amounted to 1 billion dollars last year, will be higher this year.
That means that our deficit will exceed $1 billion this year.
I continue:
Mr. Winters said he was concerned about the fall in the sale of Canadian surpluses on foreign markets.
The Minister of Finance said this afternoon that we cannot produce more than we are now producing, that we cannot produce enough to meet the demand. That means that our production is not high enough.
And now the Minister of Commerce goes to Toronto and says that we are worried about our surpluses in Canada.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
One tells us that Canada is not producing enough, that there are not enough products, and the other states that he fears we might not sell our surplus products. Who is making sense in this matter? Of the two ministers, who is lying? The Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Finance?

I think so.
Mr. Chairman, again I quote the article:
Mr. Winters said he was concerned about the decline in the sales of Canadian surplus products abroad. It is important to maintain costs and remain competitive on foreign markets.
Because taxes are an important part of costs-
That is right; remove taxes and costs will go down.
And the minister goes on to say:
Canadians should not ask so much of the federal treasury.
Canadians want nothing from the federal treasury, except what they are entitled to by the work they do to build their country, nothing more. They are not so demanding; the government is expecting more from the Canadians than the Canadians are expecting from the federal treasury.
The minister continues as follows:
If we want to avoid creating too big a gap between our taxes and those of the countries with which we are competing, the government should carefully select its spending programs and remain indifferent to pressures to spend more than it can afford.
How much can we afford? Is this, in fact, not determined by our capacity to produce?
September 8, 1966

To the extent that we produce, should we not create the capital which would enable us to sell our products? Our Canadian monetary system is only as strong as the Canadian production made by Canadians. There is no doubt about that. The more we produce, the more credit there should be available and, not restrictions on credit. And as I said a while ago, there is no economic sphere in our country unwilling to increase its production.
This is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) added:
It was hard for the Liberal members of the House of Commons to vote against the motion recently put forward by the opposition, to increase old age pensions to $100 per month from $75, as at present.
Hard as it was, the minister will tell us why he voted against a pension of $100 per month. He is very frank about it. He did not ask himself: Can Canada produce clothing and food to dress and feed adequately our older citizens, or build houses to accommodate them properly? That is not what the minister asked himself before the Canadian Club in Toronto. No, he explained why:
We wish we could have done it-
We would have been pleased to give $100 instead of $75.
-however, since it would have cost $800 million per annum and also since, even in the present circumstances, it is difficult to find enough revenues to cover our expenses at their present rate, this additional amount would have strained our economy to a point difficult to cope with.
This is the answer or the statement given by a minister regarding our senior citizens. But did the same minister oppose the interest-free loans that have been granted to foreign countries in the world?
Mr. Chairman, possibly the members of the government, the Minister of Finance, in brief, some people still find facetious the solution advocated by Social Credit-
