Mr. Chairman, I will not take advantage of my hon. colleagues' kindness and I thank them for this favour; I will not abuse their generosity.
Mr. Chairman, I have this to say: people may laugh at the suggestions made by the Creditistes, suggestions coming from the Social Credit party, Mr. Chairman, but if there are other workable and logical answers, it is time for members of the government to bring them forth. It is time for members of the government to stop running around in circles, always getting the same results. It is time members of the government went after the real troublemakers, namely the financiers; they are the ones responsible for inflation, and responsible for misery in times of plenty, responsible for poverty in many areas of Canada. The hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette) brought up the question at noon, and he was right; I congratulate him for the question he put on the order paper.
Mr. Chairman, we speak of war on poverty. How is it that the government who has promised us to wage war on poverty is today asking us to tighten our belts, rich and poor alike, or simply calls for more poor people, as my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) says, instead of making war against poverty? These statements which the minister made this afternoon mean a war against the poor; war against the poor people, that is the path along which we are presently treading.
Mr. Chairman, when a financial system is elaborated which at all times will place in the hands of the Canadian people a purchasing power corresponding to Canadian productivity no more but no less, and when we resort to the distribution of a national dividend based on this productivity, made available to each and everyone of the Canadian citizens, we will have accomplished something. In one year it will be the same old story, in two, ten years we will still be faced with the same gaps, the same situation, just as we have had to put up with this situation ever since Confederation. We will not give relief to the Canadian people with debts and interest on imaginary debts; we will help them by turning over to them what is theirs by right and in justice, and this is what members of the Ralliement are trying to do.

September 8, 1968
Supply-Finance
The only thing I wish is that members on both sides of the house consider other proposals than those brought forward by the minister. Let hon. members propose something else; let us stop imposing sacrifices and let it be clear, once and for all, that Canada is capable of providing an honest affluence to each and everyone of her citizens, that Canada is capable of providing security with personal freedom.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
After listening to the statement of the Minister of Finance this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, and the speeches of the representatives of the different parties on the opposition side, I can only say that this is a discouraging debate upon which we have now entered. It is discouraging because as we look back at the last election campaign and the one previous to that, we find that we were told over and over again that the Liberal party had the answer to the economic problems of this country. They were going to completely reverse the trends of recent years and we would be on our way to perpetual prosperity. After listening to the Minister of Finance, I find that he has actually become an apologist for the very policies he used to criticize. It is obvious he has been unable to come up with anything different. He says that we must tighten our belts; that we are now headed into a dangerous economic period.
It is stated that Canada now faces the worst inflationary spiral since the end of the last boom in 1957. Today the Minister of Finance lined himself up with those who see a great economic crisis just ahead. He has joined with those who see disaster, and well he should because if we continue as we have been without coming up with a different type of financial policy, whether it be fiscal or monetary, we are headed for economic disaster. In order to ward off this danger, the government has reversed its policies of less than a year ago. It has become painfully obvious now that in the internal struggles in the Liberal party so far as financial policies are concerned, the orthodoxy of the Minister of Finance has come out on top. It is not a very happy picture, Mr. Chairman. If this so-called inflationary situation should continue, the Canadian people will be robbed of millions of dollars. Those who live on fixed incomes, those who are not able to do anything about increasing their earnings, such as old age

pensioners and farmers, will find themselves in a more difficult situation.
The end result will be that we will be completely priced out of the world markets. We are going to find ourselves suffering from a lack of markets and from unemployment. I am convinced that unless something different is tried, unless some different financial policy is implemented, then it will be only a matter of months until we will be in the same position as Great Britain is in today. I agree with the minister when he says our basic economic problems are twofold. The first is the longer term problem of educating and adapting our great labour force, as well as improving our capital resources to meet the opportunities present in our modern world. Second, there is the shorter term problem of preventing excessive total expenditures, excessive increases in prices and costs of production. True, within the framework of the policies the minister outlined in his first budget, and as he outlined again tonight, these are our basic problems.
However, they need not be our basic problems if we had different financial policies. We, in Social Credit, disagree completely with the proposed cure. As we interpret what the minister has said, it seems to us that he is intent on only diagnosing the symptoms of the disease and not considering its source, the basic cause of the economic sickness that is presently upon us is completely ignored. In no way is he coming to grips with the basic problems. If this course is continued, then in my opinion the affluent Canadian society faces a financial crisis that will make the thirties look like a picnic. Because of the uncertainty that is evident within the economy today, and the prospect of a bust following the present boom, we could tip over into a depression. Then, our financial institutions, as they exist today, would collapse and 75 per cent of everything we own, along with the mortgage companies, would be lost. This country faces a pretty grim prospect.
The minister says that the Canadian people will suffer if a continued boom should lead to a bust. Why should there be a continuous boom and bust cycle in the economy with the tremendous resources that we have, with our ability and our know-how, with our ability to consume and with the markets of the world reaching out to us? Why should there not be a continuous development and growth in our economy? So long as we continue to use the policies that are advocated by the present
September 8, 1966

.government, and they are basically no different from the policies of the administration before them, we face the prospect of a continuing boom and bust cycle.
What we have been trying to say for many years in Social Credit, and we say it again now, is that with a different fiscal policy and with a logical monetary policy-you cannot separate the two-there is absolutely no need for the boom and bust cycle of the present orthodox economic policies that we have had since long before world war I. Until we wake up and realize that there is a new approach; until we understand that the old system that has been geared to production, while it has performed a useful purpose in the past, is inadequate to meet the problems of a society that has solved the problem of production; until we face the basic problem of distribution, then we will continue to bungle along toward the economic chaos and confusion that threatens us today.
In his statement tonight, the minister said that we are now producing about all we can in Canada this year. This is a false statement, Mr. Chairman. We can increase the productive capacity of this country by 50 per cent within two years. We would not have to worry about where we were going to get the resources or where we were going to get the manpower to do it. Just the other day, I was reading a report from one of our automobile manufacturing companies. This report stated that company could increase the productive capacity of its factories by 50 per cent and not add more than 10 per cent to the labour force, and without adding any new equipment. It is untrue to say we have reached our productive capacity in this country. The things that people need to live form just a fraction of our potential productive capacity. In a world that is starving, in a world that cannot find enough to meet the needs of its people, the greatest challenge that faces Canada is to move out and become not only the breadbasket of the world but the source of know-how to help other countries increase their own food production. This is our challenge; this is our world mission.
We are faced with the prospect of one of the largest grain crops we have ever had in Canada. We could produce to capacity in every area of agriculture within a couple of years if we could be assured of the markets that are waiting beyond our shores. There are millions and millions of starving people today in the southern hemisphere and on the Indian
Supply-Finance
subcontinent and many other parts of the world who need what we have.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The minister talks about price controls. During the war price controls worked pretty well and perhaps they were necessary in a wartime economy. But do we have to resort once more to controls which not only limit our production but also our distributive capacity, simply because we refuse to face up to the basic economic reforms that are necessary to make a system which has been developed over the years just a little bit better, and which put it in tune with and on the same wavelength with automation and cybernation, which come to us as a blessing?
When I hear hon. members talk about full employment it seems to me they are closing their eyes to the facts. What we should be looking for today is not for the myth of full employment but for full unemployment. That is the blessing that can come if only we can use the productive capacities which we have developed and which are at our fingertips. The fact is that the day of full employment in the sense of working a 40 hour week 12 months in the year will have gone, if we can put our productive capacity to work.
With our ability to produce ought to come that leisure which will improve our culture, which will permit us once again to enter into the era of art and refinement and cultural development for which we do not have time today as we try to survive and keep enough food in our stomachs and sufficient clothes on our backs.
The minister talks of restricting expansion. He has cancelled the medicare program of the government. Why did he not cut down government expenditure last March? He outlined in his statement today that government expenditure this year is going to be $8,600 million. True the government has cut back on certain phases of development. I believe what if we really wanted to get down to help the present situation we are facing under the orthodox framework put forward by the minister, the first step would be to control and to hold steady on government expenditure.
In his statement today the minister said that the anticipated deficit is $300 million. What happened as a result of the first budget brought down by the minister? Income tax was increased for six persons out of ten; business has been forced to put 5 per cent of its cash into compulsory savings; it restrained new projects. Yet the minister brought in a

September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
budget which showed an increase over the previous year's budget of approximately 10 per cent.
These are questions which are difficult to answer. I believe that we have to come back to basics. There is a lot of talk about inflation. The word "inflation" is used by the minister and by every newspaper today. Every speech relating to the economy of the country includes the word "inflation".
Inflation in its true sense means that we have too much money. Too many dollars are chasing too few goods. We do not have inflation in this country today in the orthodox sense of the word. To use that word is to raise a banner which gives a false impression. What we have today is tight money-deflation.
As far as our monetary situation is concerned-and inflation usually means money problems-what we have is deflation, not enough money to finance the development of our resources and to carry on the expansion of our industries, to finance our trade policies, particularly as they relate to some of the newer nations of the world. But we do not have inflation.
In this regard I agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands when he says that the government is going to have to decide whether to face up to an economic problem which really is inflation, or whether it will have to face up to something else which is sending the cost of everything which we buy higher and higher. If it is inflation that we have, it is an inflation of prices, an inflation of our cost of living. It has nothing to do with the inflation of money; it has to do with deflationary monetary policies.
It was also said that we must deal with fiscal policies, placing the emphasis there rather than on monetary policies. It is the government which decides both financial policies and fiscal policies, and the two cannot be separated. Until we bring in financial reform and combine the two with some logical fiscal reform, the problem will never be solved.
I believe that if we are to face up to the realities as they present themselves today, we will have to quit hiding behind phrases which deceive the public and which coerce them to go along with policies which perhaps are necessary within the framework of orthodoxy that the minister presented to us tonight but which are absolutely unnecessary on the basis of logic and reason.
What we are facing in Canada today is a price explosion. Our cost of living goes up

and up. I want to say right now that at the root of this problem is the debt system. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle made an eloquent speech but he did not get down to any different approach. He merely talked in political terms so as to defend what happened under the last administration in light of what is happening now.
During the less than five years of that administration there was a governmental deficit in the country on the federal level as it relates to direct debt, foreign debt and balance of trade of more than $5 billion. That was accounted for in less than five years, and it now is going on and on. With it goes the cost of servicing the debt. If we did not have to pay the $1,180 million that we paid last year by way of interest, where would our deficit be today? Gone.
Why is it necessary to have deficit financing? If perchance the argument that the minister put forward tonight is correct, it seems to me that the first step which he should take as far as governmental expenditures for which he is responsible are concerned is to balance his budget this year.
In addition to this there is the matter of private debt, corporate debt and mortgage debt. The handmaiden of debt is higher taxation-you cannot get away from that. Taxes will inevitably go up. Behind the inflationary crisis we are facing is this cause. It is neither the profits which the corporations make nor the wages that the working people must demand through their labour organizations, or strikes. These are merely the symptoms of something which is much deeper. If the cost of living continues to go up, then the income in the pockets of the people must go up in proportion, or their standard of living will go down.
Along with this is the simple fact that we operate in this country on a debt policy which requires deficit financing on one hand and gross indebtedness on the private sector on the other hand, supported by a continually spiralling increase in the tax load that we carry.
Our budget this year at the federal level is over $8.5 billion. When we get the supplementary estimates that we can expect, the figure will be well over $9 billion and on the way to $10 billion. If we combine this with the cost of municipal and provincial government in this country we reach a figure that is not very far short of $20 billion for governmental expenditure alone.
September 8, 196S

We in this country are grossly over-governed. Compare that figure with the net national earnings in this country-not the gross national product but net national earnings, money coming into the pockets of the Canadian people, whether by way of commissions, the sale of produce, salaries, or what have you. Last year this figure was about $41 billion. Let us suppose that this figure increases by a reasonable amount this year; to be liberal in our estimate, let us say $43 billion is the figure for this year. What percentage of that figure is taken up with expenditure on government at the different levels? It is more than 45 per cent. In other words, more than 45 cents of every dollar which we earn goes to pay for the cost of government.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
History will tell us, if we read history correctly, that no free country, no free society has ever survived when the cost of government has exceeded 50 per cent of the earnings of the people of that society. At more than 45 per cent, this is the problem we face today. This is something that must change. If the minister had really wanted to deal with this inflationary situation as it relates to the cost of living, this situation which has brought about tight money that at the present time we have in Canada, then, I think, the first thing he might have done would have been to hold firm on government expenditures, at least.
Let us look at the picture from a very elementary point of view. It is good to be elementary once in a while. Our problem in Canada is not production. We can produce far more than we are producing. We, perhaps more than any other nation-and I say this even considering the economic wealth of the United States-have solved the problem of production. Neither is our problem consumption. Sure, our standard of living has gone up, but there is nothing wrong with that. If we have the natural resources, the ability and the will to develop those natural resources, why should not our standard of living go up? Why should not every family have a home? There is nothing wrong with having a two-car garage, if that is the standard of living we want.
Our problem is not consumption. Even if we had solved that, and were consuming to our capacity, what about the millions of others in the world who go hungry? No, the
Supply-Finance
problem is not consumption at all. Our problem today is one of distribution. We have not solved the economics of distribution. We are trying to apply those economics to a debt system that was geared to production in the days when there was a scarcity, and when we could not produce enough to meet our needs. We had to adapt ourselves to the conditions of the economy at that time. But conditions have changed.
Bring in a monetary policy which will cure the problems of distribution, and all these problems will disappear, as will the booms and busts of our economic system. Instead, there will be a logical and steady growth, even as every living organism must grow.
Beyond this debt picture that we have been talking about is the monetary policy that brings money into our economy. But the essential function that that money performs is that of a debt. They ridicule us, in this party, for talking about debt free money. But money was never intended to be a commodity. It is because we try to make it a commodity that we find ourselves in our present difficulties. Money is a service, a service through which we distribute our wealth, by which we are able to produce the wealth that others may consume.
It is necessary to bring our financial and monetary policies up to date, in an era where the production potential has reached tremendous heights, where there is automation and cybernation, in order for those to be geared to the distribution problems which we have. Yes, we demoralize our people. We demoralize our people today so that we, who as a people have more insurance per capita than any other people in the world, are not willing to invest our own savings in the development of our own resources. We go out and invest in our debts, instead. We hear criticism about so much United States ownership of Canadian industry. The truth of the matter is that for every per capita dollar the United States invests in Canada, three per capita Canadian dollars are invested in the United States. That is done because we do not have confidence in our own country.
Apply this regionally, and look at the west where productive capacity has expanded at an unprecedented rate, both in relation to the population and the economy at large. We do not even have financial policy here in the east, where our fiscal policies are made, where our financial centres are, to encourage investment in the west of our country.

September 8, 1966
Supply-Finance
The other day the government cancelled plans for a pipe line that was to pass through part of the United States, a pipe line that opens unlimited markets for Canadian gas across the border, and would benefit the Ontario user of gas by lowering the price which he would have to pay. In other words, we cut it off. It does not suit our national interest to let it go across the border-never mind the economy. I sometimes wonder if the government is not afraid of another pipe line debate, and rather than let the matter come before the house it disposed of the matter before it got here.
We discourage the investment of our own savings in our own resources. What we need in this country is a stable financial policy that will give us a stable dollar. We have a stable yard; we have a stable pound; we have a stable gallon. Why cannot we have a stable dollar? Why do we have to rob the generations of the future of the savings which have been put away for them today? Why do we have to rob our older citizens, our senior citizens, of their hard-earned savings that they have put away for their latter years? Why should we destroy our own savings? Why are we using a system in which a dollar is a debt dollar, which depreciates in value every year, so that over every ten or 15 year period we know it will be worth 25 per cent less? That is what the cost of living is doing to our dollar today. Why cannot we have a financial policy that will give us a stable dollar; a dollar that is worth a dollar today, tomorrow, next year and ten years from now. It can be done.
One would think with all the ability displayed on the front benches of the government, that something helpful could be defined. I do not care if it is called Social Credit, or anything else. That is not the point. We need a fiscal policy that will work, that will encourage our own people to invest, not in debts of yesterday-no-but in the prospects of an unprecedented productive tomorrow.
Today in Canada our most valuable resource is our own credit. That is something which ought to be used, and used, with the resourcefulness of our own people. Why cannot we use our own credit and our own resources, for the benefit of our own people? That we do not is a paradox.
I would say in closing-my time is nearly up-that the number of ridiculous paradoxes in our economy shows that it is redirection we need, rather than reduced speed. Why

dampen the boom? The construction industry is forced to slow down because of manpower shortages. Nevertheless the cost of governmental administration grows by leaps and bounds, to meet the needs of the new welfare state measures. We are urged to buy Canadian assets back from the United States, but the provisions of our present financial policies make it necessary for our industry to turn to the United States for the kind of risk capital it needs. That is why the west is moving forward; it is not because it is disloyal to Canada, but because the financial centres of the east do not have the vision necessary for the nation.
Why cannot we use our own credit, and our own capital. Canadians invest in the national debt because the return is more secure than from an investment in resource development. Though it is necessary to improve our balance of payments problem, tight money policies and taxation tend to put our producers in a non-competitive position. As I say, the problem is not that of production, but rather the facilitating of measures to enable the distribution of what we are able to produce.
An economist recently commented that we are learning to live with prosperity but we do not know as much about managing it as we do about getting there. Our need in Canada is not to hold back, but to move ahead. In the distribution of goods and services we are in a field where we are just beginning to tap our potential. We pat ourselves on the back for being good businessmen, but we rationalize our dollars-those dollars which have been expended, which have been invested-as being good dollars. At the same time our trade deficits grow and our production slows down.
We slow down the building industry. Today, in Canada, apartment occupancy is at 99 per cent. It is easy to cut a building program off; it takes much longer to get it going again. The disposing of surpluses is a narrow and old fashioned way of assessing our tremendous production potential.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
What about those many countries which do not have enough to eat? What about world markets for our primary and secondary products? The time has come to institute policies which go beyond the mere sale of surplus commodities or the cutting back of productive capacity.
September 8, 1966

Finally, we need to make advances in the field of distribution, moving goods from where-ever they are produced to wherever they are needed. World trade on a new basis for international settlement presents another challenge. We cannot continue in this regard as we have done in the past in the face of one of the greatest challenges of our generation.
Only when all Canadians have an adequate standard of living, only when all Canadians are adequately housed and properly fed, can we adopt the attitudes which have been expounded tonight and pat ourselves on the back. Only when trading policies are developed which are capable of channeling our surplus goods to the needy populations of the developing countries will we be able to congratulate ourselves on what we have achieved. In the meantime, there are too many things to be done, for us to express approval of the financial policy which we have heard enunciated tonight.

Mr. Chairman, our primary concern when debating this problem of inflation tonight is its effect upon the Canadian people. While I do not belong to the generation which remembers the kind of inflation which occurred in Germany between the two wars, even those of my years are reminded of those days when the people of Germany had, literally, to take their money to market in wheelbarrows. It is because we recognize that inflation affects each and every citizen of this country that every member of this house is taking the present debate very seriously.
I should like to point out that those who suffer most from the effects of inflation are, almost invariably, the poor-those families which are locked in poverty, deprivation or destitution. Time and time again hon. members belonging to the New Democratic Party have recognized that when inflation strikes it strikes with greatest force at such things as food, clothing and housing, all of them nonluxury items, essential items which vitally concern those who are perhaps less fortunate than ourselves.
What I found most disturbing about the minister's speech this afternoon was the fact-and many hon. members have already mentioned this-that he had decided to adopt negative, old fashioned methods of coping with modern problems. Invariably the solutions he proposed in his statement this afternoon, the horse-and-buggy methods which he
Supply-Finance
has in mind, are bound to adversely affect the poor, the destitute and the deprived more than any others in this country. Those who are living on fixed or on shrinking incomes, those who are already suffering from the serious inroads of inflation, will be even more seriously affected by the measures which the minister has proposed today.
As my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle so ably said a few moments ago, instead of relying on this negative, horse-and-buggy approach the minister should be enunciating a system of positive politics and policies to deal with modern problems.
We are told that the parents of school children will have to pay up to 15 per cent more for school clothing compared with a year ago. That is the amount of increase in the price of shoes and all the other things needed before children can be sent back to school. What about food prices. Last year, processed cheese cost 39 cents a pound. This year the price is 41 cents. The price of cheddar cheese last year was 65 cents. This year, it is 69 cents. A pound of bacon cost 89 cents last year. Now it costs $1.39. Corn cost 35 cents a dozen, peeled. This year the price is 49 cents.
Every housewife who went to the supermarket last week knows these things. A ten-dollar basket of groceries a year ago cost $13.08 today. Is there a single measure announced by the minister today which is likely to alleviate this situation? I say that the negative, bureaucratic methods of approach adopted by the minister will not even begin to solve the problem of inflation which is besetting the Canadian people.
The minister told us: We are doing pretty well, compared with other countries. We hear such things said time and time again. Sir, when I bring this statement to the attention of my constituents and of other Canadians in all walks of life, they tell me they do not care what is going on in other countries. They say it is our job here in Canada to solve Canadian problems. The fact that other countries are not doing well is no excuse for us to say we can do badly. It is rather like finding satisfaction in the fact that a deskmate has flunked his examinations when you yourself have failed. And the minister is going to fail his examination in tackling inflation if he thinks for one moment that these negative policies of his will work out satisfactorily. They will not.
In outlining the principles of inflation the minister told us that basically speaking we

are faced with long-term problems and shortterm problems. The long-term problems includes automation, technical training, and preparing our work force for new roles in a scientific age. But though he said these things this afternoon, what were the first two priorities to be cut in the short-term program?
We were told we could expect cuts in assistance to research. We were told that the provision of scholarships to universities would be delayed. In other words, it is as if the minister were telling a runner to put on heavy working boots rather than running shoes before trying to win a mile race.
Everyone in this house realizes that while Britain spends $5 per scientist and the United States between $10 and $15, Canada spends only $1 per scientist. Everyone recognizes that government, which has a vital and genuine role to play in positive policies as a means of combating inflation, will have to increase, and increase again, the amount of its assistance to research.

We have a terrible situation in Canada, where we are losing doctors and medical personnel because we have not supported research in our universities. Yet, of all things, the minister places at the top of his list of cutbacks today assistance to research and education, two primary measures which we must bolster if in a long-term manner we are going to combat the problems of inflation. This is a paradox which I do not believe the government can explain away.
This country is going to be in serious trouble in terms of inflation, in terms of our economic approach to Canadian problems unless we drastically step up our assistance to research; but the government has told us today that, along with postponing assistance to higher education, research is going to get the axe.
I can quite understand the minister saying we must deal with short-term measures; but his negative short-term measures, plus the fact that they interfere with the long-term measures we need to combat inflation, are not the answer. Everybody in this House of Commons who talks with constituents in the lower income brackets, people who have a motivation upwards to better their role in Canada, recognizes that housing, clothing, education and foodstuffs are the main things in their economic picture. But what are we told? Not only does inflation affect the poor, but it is mainly the poor, the deprived and the

destitute who are told to buckle their belts in the program the minister has announced.
What the minister told us today in effect is that the reactionary right-wing group in the Liberal party is finally triumphant; and that, Mr. Chairman, is one of the reasons I quit that party 12 years ago. I realized that this was going to happen. I recognized that when loyal and excellent civil servants like the Minister of Finance and half the range of the front bench finally took over control of the Liberal party, along with the rest of the establishment, that would be the victory of the right-wing, and it has happened today. Where are all the young, forward-looking members in the Liberal party? They are not in the chamber tonight supporting the minister, because not for one minute do they believe in the policies he has enunciated.
Where is the Minister of National Health and Welfare ever since he was told summarily this afternoon that medicare was now in limbo?

approach-will not satisfy very many Canadians when they read about it tomorrow morning.
Rather than emphasize a negative approach, let us talk about the positive things we can do in the short-term and in the long-term to combat inflation. I for one do not believe, for example, that housing should be considered in the cyclical approach to combat inflation. Canada is almost the sole country in the modern western world that has not a public or quasi public approach to housing.
Housing is not always considered as a social welfare measure, but at least in western Europe and in most countries in the modern western world it has never been taken into governmental plans in terms of combatting inflation. Today thousands upon thousands of young and middle-aged Canadians are looking for proper housing, but last year 85 per cent of the housing loans made by C.M.H.C. were to Canadians with incomes of $6,000 and upwards.
What are we doing for the poorer people in this country who want decent housing? Our negative, dinosaur Minister of Labour-God Almighty, when will he resign; it won't be too soon for me-not only has ruined labour-management relations but has no housing policy. He and the rest of the ex-bureaucrats sitting on the treasury benches are telling the poorer people of Canada that because of inflation and their own old establishment method of dealing with it, they are not going to have any more houses.
What is happening today? There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians, young and middle-aged, who are looking for houses, but the government tells them the situation is going to be much, much worse before it gets better because we have to combat inflation.

I cannot find all the statistics I have gathered on this matter at the moment but I do have a note here which says, for example, that in 1961 when Britain spent $3.15 per capita on public housing, and the United States .08 cents per capita, Canada spent only .10 cents per capita. The fact is that we have no housing policy for people in the lower income groups. I suggest that the government should devise a public housing policy in the very near future to deal with this problem, because that coupled with what is happening in rising prices for foodstuffs and clothing, all essential, nonluxury items, affect those people who should be least affected in the whole, total picture of inflation.

This is one more reason that we should convene as quickly as possible a conference to modernize our constitution so that Canada will have a modern constitution to deal with modern problems in modern times. I asked the Prime Minister whether we could anticipate something being done about old age pensions in this part of the present session. Mr. Speaker, as soon as we complete consideration of the railway legislation it is my intention to make a statement in the house about the priority attached to the other pieces of legislation to be dealt with during this part of the session. The medicare legislation will be included in that list.

Yesterday, in the absence of the Prime Minister, I asked the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Martin) if he could tell us on what day that statement by the Prime Minister would be made. He asked me to wait until today. I asked the question again today. We had an interesting and amiable exchange, but got no information. I suppose, Mr. Speaker, I will be told that I have had my answer in the statement made today by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). I suggest that today's statement is not an answer to the questions I put to the Prime Minister asking him for a statement to the house as to the government's legislative intentions.
We have been told, of course, by the Minister of Finance that the government intends to go ahead with medicare legislation.
[Mr. Mongrain.J

Oh yes, we are told it is going to be put through at this session. But the effective date is to be changed from July 1, 1967, to July 1, 1968. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this way of stringing the house and the country along has gone on far too long in Canada. With respect to old age pensions, again we have been strung along. Today, the Minister of Finance talked about the income guarantee program, and we know that is the name the government applies to its old age pension proposal. However, today we were not told what would be the effective date of whatever program the government proposes to introduce.
Now, despite the answer given today by the Minister of Finance I still put my question. We, in this house, are conscious of the number of times that this government has had to change its position, the number of times it has had to retreat. I suggest that the public outcry will call for a change on these two points. The government cannot get away with no action, not even a statement to us, on the old age pension question. The government cannot get away with another year's delay in medicare. To say that these things are inflationary is utter nonsense. They are the least inflationary expenditures the government could make, namely money for old people to buy the necessities of life and a medicare program which simply redistributes the way in which we spend our money on medical care.
I suggest, therefore, that my question still stands. May I put it to the Acting Prime Minister, or whichever minister is going to answer it, in this way: Are you going to raise old age pensions in this session? Are you going to stick to July 1, 1967, as the effective date for medicare? Or are you going to let the brunt of the high cost of living fall most heavily on the people with medical bills and on our senior citizens? It is not good enough for the government to pull the rug out from under its ministers, to pull the rug out from under the people of this country. If we are going to have respect for parliament, let us stand by our commitments. I ask the government tonight what it is really going to do on these two issues: an immediate increase in the old age pension and standing by the effective date of July 1, 1967, for medicare?

Speaker, with your kind permission I will try to make my remarks in English in response to my colleagues in the house who occasionally display a lot of effort in extending this same courtesy to the French speaking members when they try to speak French. Therefore I beg the indulgence of the house, because I am not a master of the English vocabulary and cannot speak it as well as French.
This afternoon I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question as a result of seeing something in the papers today. He had announced during a dinner for a French minister that the government is considering offering to six French libraries in
DEBATES	8247

I am not trying to be destructively critical; I am just trying to give an opportunity to the government to clarify the situation and perhaps give more information to the public.
I should like to know from the minister or his parliamentary assistant when the government plans to make this gift of books. Second, what will be the proportion of French books and English books? Third, who will be in charge of choosing the French books, and what kind of French books are to be considered? Will they be novels, detective stories, best sellers, or will they be about all kinds of subjects so as to give an idea of our Canadian culture, if there is any? I suppose these books will be bought through Canadian booksellers. I should like the government to assure us of this fact. I conclude my remarks by saying that this is a very constructive move. This is very good public relations and I am sure all members of the house will want to congratulate the government for doing what it has done.

I would like to thank my colleague for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) who was kind enough to ask his question in English and I would like to return the compliment in the best Canadian tradition by answering in French.
Mr. Speaker, that project has been devised to put at the disposal of the French public in general, such as specialists, scholars and researchers, the bulk of our publications in the main fields of culture in Canada. It is part of the cultural agreement signed by France and Canada on November 17, 1965.
The books were chosen by experts in our National Library in consultation with the services of the Department of External Affairs, taking into account the standards used in libraries. The proportion of French books is approximately 65 per cent.
Virtually all areas of Canadian culture are represented: French and English Canadian literature, history, geography, sociology, economics, politics, philosophy, science etc.

The National Library has already acquired most of the selected titles and is now busy with the listing and labelling. As soon as the department and the French authorities, working in co-operation, have made their choice of the recipient libraries, we will proceed with the distribution of collections. In this connection, the departmental officers took advantage of the presence in Ottawa of the French Minister of Education, Mr. Christian Fouchet, to establish the facts of the question with him today. He promised he would soon communicate to us the list of libraries suggested by the French authorities.
We are of the opinion that this presentation of books should contribute to make Canadian culture better known in France and to bring our two countries closer.
The possibility is not excluded, subject to the means at our disposal, that we may consider, if such were the desire of French authorities, bringing up to date later the collections that we are about to offer the French government.

This question was prompted by two very pompous statements which have been made, one in Toronto and one in Montreal, by two officials connected with professional hockey in this country.
Carl Brewer is a man of 27 years of age who during the past season attended the University of Toronto. He has been asked to accept a position on the Canadian national hockey team which will be competing for the world championship in Europe and he has been very anxious to accept such an opportunity. subtopic: UNDERTAKING BY C.P.R. TO PAY MUNICIPAL TAXES IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY COMPANY

speechtext:
Montreal, August 29, 1966
Ian D. Sinclair,
President
Dear Mr. Pickersgill:
You will recall conversations we have held over some months relative to whether as a contribution to the rationalization of Canadian transportation legislation, Canadian Pacific would be prepared voluntarily to forgo the perpetual exemption from municipal taxation provided in Clause 16 of its contract of 21st October, 1880, which is the Schedule to the Canadian Pacific Railway Act, S.C. (1881) Chap. 1.
This exemption from municipal taxation applies to the main line of Canadian Pacific outside of the boundaries of the original "Postage Stamp" Province of Manitoba, across Saskatchewan and Alberta. This exemption has contractual, statutory and consti-titional validity.
One of the points that you raised in our
discussions was that the exemption imposed a burden upon the affected municipalities which is not borne by other municipalities on the Canadian Pacific system. You also raised the point that a perpetual provision such as that referred to did not take into account changes and varying circumstances which had occurred in the many years since the contract was executed by Canadian Pacific and the Government of Canada.
I have discussed the matter with the Directors of the Company and they have authorized me to say that, under the arrangement hereinafter mentioned, the Company is
prepared to forgo voluntarily perpetual exemption from taxation by the local authorities on our main line in the Prairie Provinces in three equal stages: one-third for the year commencing January 1 after legislation is enacted modernizing and rationalizing existing legislation and taking into account, among other things, the effective changed conditions on freight rates otherwise fixed; a further one-third in the succeeding year; the balance in the third year from the commencement of the period as stated.
The Canadian Pacific proposes that the Government of Canada ascertain from the municipalities involved the municipal taxes that would have been payable, subject to statutory procedures as to assessment appeals, had the exemption not been in effect. When this amount has been determined, Canadian Pacific would make a grant of an equal amount to Her Majesty the Queen in the right of Canada for distribution to the municipalities involved in such manner as the Government of Canada might from time to time deem appropriate.
At any time after the expiry of the period indicated above, the Canadian Pacific would have no objection to action being taken to amend the constitution and the legislation to terminate the perpetual exemption from local taxation referred to.
You are free to make the position of Canadian Pacific public whenever it seems to you desirable to do so in the public interest.
Yours very truly,
Ian D. Sinclair
Hon. J. W. Pickersgill,
Minister of Transport,
Parliament Buildings,
OTTAWA, Ont.
